question: Reveal character through what the character does in the dramatized action itself, rather than telling the reader who they are.
Check the causality of your story: action is “this happened, then that,” plot is “this happened because that”—rewrite the sequence so later events happen because of earlier ones.
Find an alternation between scene and summary, showing and telling, somewhere on the spectrum of predominance.
Create tension by setting a character's appearance against their actions—an elegantly dressed woman tearing yellowed newspaper into strips—and let the disparity make the reader wonder.
For each scene, ask what it is really about, what is at stake, and how it contributes to the piece; the answers tell you what to cut, keep, develop, or drop.
Stop polishing and just start: any way in is a good way in—begin at a place, a moment, a scene, or a voice that excites you, and find your way from there.
Check whether your beginning sets up a contrast with what unfolds later, so the early lightness or forgiveness makes the coming darkness land harder.
If you're writing a crime drama, start with the crime or its discovery in scene before pulling back into summary to introduce the detectives—the unanswered who and why will draw the reader on.
Check your opening against the general demands of beginnings: does it draw readers into the world through setting, situation, or character, and give them a reason to keep reading?

If the beginning still doesn't work, move it to another juncture: write a scene or summary that occurs before or after your current opening, or try starting from a different character's point of view.
Don't force your beginning early—accept that many writers only find their true opening after the draft is finished, when plot and ending are known.
Open with an unanswered question, presented through showing or telling, so the reader keeps going to find the answer.
Answer for yourself the questions readers bring to your opening: what world have they entered, what and who matters, why they matter, and who is guiding them through the tale.
Start your piece with scene or summary—either can work—as long as the opening meets the general demands of beginnings and the specific demands of your tale.
Before you craft the final version of your first pages, pin down what's at stake in the piece and what its themes are—until you know, the perfect beginning can't come.

If you've shaped your beginning to set up what will follow but aren't satisfied, rephrase it in the other narrative mode—switch scene for summary or vice versa—to get the needed distance or closeness.
Open with a character whose presentation and true nature conflict—the tension between what she presents and who she is draws the reader in.
In a story set in an alternate reality, spend time establishing the world in summary before introducing characters and situations, so the fantastic elements are easier to accept.
After a stretch of fast-paced action, give readers breathing space with a slower section—scene or summary.
Keep digressive reflection to about a paragraph, then bring the narrative elements back into play—don’t interrupt the story for too long.
Open a story with a brief omniscient reflective passage—a paragraph or two—then slide into the mind of the protagonist.
Rewrite any character whose wisdom or behavior doesn't fit their age and experience, such as children who are preternaturally smarter than their parents.
Analyze a scene from a writer you admire: map how it is built and how it shows rather than tells, then apply that structure to your own scene.
Rewrite any dialogue where characters speak outside their own idiom, keeping each voice true to how that person actually talks.
Cut cliché, sentimental images like 'a single tear ran down her cheek' from your scenes.
Check your scenes for continuity contradictions — details like a character's family or circumstances shifting with no explanation — and fix them.
When you are moved by a scene you've written, ask yourself whether the emotional intensity feels earned — does it match the level of intensity you actually felt?
Create a brief scene in which conflict between two characters is apparent, whether small (a choice of restaurant) or large (a divorce).

Eavesdrop on a conversation you can hear but not see, then write the dialogue so the speakers' relationship, power dynamic, and individual voices come through their words alone — identify the agenda and any conflict in the exchange.
Rephrase the obvious comparisons in your work with fresh, surprising similes — write a list of ten and keep the strongest.
Rewrite a scene from a different point of view — if you wrote it in third person, switch to first, or change the point-of-view character — and see what the shift reveals.
Choose one detail of appearance, gesture, voice, or action for each character that reveals something important about them, and write a scene in which those details carry the characterization.
Rewrite one of your scenes in a different season and time of day — early evening in winter versus mid-morning in summer — and consider how time and setting affect mood and tone.
Write a scene in present tense, then rewrite it in past tense, and compare how the tense shift alters the tone.
Rephrase dialogue that delivers exposition the characters would already know, making it sound like natural speech.
Rewrite your first-person narrator's attitude so they come across as self-aware rather than self-pitying or self-aggrandizing, so readers trust the emotions and facts.
Signal an unreliable narrator deliberately, or don't use one at all: don't risk the reader's trust by making your narrator too self-regarding or too villainous to believe.
Cut or summarize any scene in which no important events or interactions ensue — nothing that reveals character or advances plot or themes.
Scan your work for passages where you've taken on the style and mannerisms of a writer you admire, and rewrite them in your own voice.
When a scene does little to heighten complications or further plot or themes, summarize it instead of dramatizing it — keep a quiet scene only as setup for what comes later.
Read your dialogue aloud; wherever you stumble over the words your characters are speaking, revise the line.
Articulate the difference between sentiment and sentimentality in your work — name where genuine emotion ends and the attempt to manipulate the reader begins.
Rewrite any death or parting scene that relies on tearjerker conventions — the dying person as an angel, a deathbed conversion, last-minute forgiveness — so the emotion feels earned.
Replace a random detail in a summary with one whose associations reinforce the character or situation you are writing about.
Expand a flat summary with concrete specifics that let the reader infer more than facts alone, such as the trouble of heating stones in a fire to warm a child’s hands.
Replace an overused detail like a hunched old lady or verdant landscape with a fresh image that makes the subject vivid.
Choose details of behavior or appearance that expose your character’s inner life, like a man careful not to step on cracks.
Go through your summaries and make each detail do more than one job: reveal character or further theme, not merely inform.
Add sensory detail—sights and sounds—to a flat summary until it reads as vividly as a scene.
Animate one summary detail with a simile to make it memorable, as when potted plants “sat like faithful dwarfs.”
Add a detail that raises an unanswered question to create tension in the summary.
Audit each concrete detail in your summaries: besides giving information, does it advance the theme?
Rephrase narration with everyday, repeated phrasing like “before that” to give it a conversational, informal quality.
Shift your first-person narrator’s language from simple to more complex over the course of the work to show growing age or sophistication.
Set your summary’s tone through word choice and sentence structure: ordinary words for an informal, conversational feel.
Replace clichéd metaphor or simile in your summaries with fresh symbolic language that suits the material it illustrates.
Cut each interjection of an older, wiser perspective unless it furthers the reader’s understanding of character and situation in an essential way.
Question the placement of each older-narrator interjection: could the information sit elsewhere, or must it interrupt the younger narrator’s story right here?
Layer your first-person narrative so summaries reveal how your narrator sees the world at different ages and stages of maturity.
Check whether you are using irony or humor to avoid emotion on painful material, and rewrite so the fear stays visible underneath the jokes.
Establish your piece’s tone and mood deliberately in your summaries, where they first take hold.
Name your intended tone with a precise adjective—urgent, dismissive, ironic, mocking—then check that the wording actually produces it.
Cut or temper any tone that detracts from or overwhelms the material it is meant to carry.
If you address a harsh, judgmental tone directly to “you,” reconsider: such address risks making readers turn away.
Rephrase a line so its tone shifts—say it with enthusiasm, then with dismissal—and find the wording that carries the meaning you intend.
Make sure change occurs in your scene—in characters, in circumstances, or in the reader’s perceptions—since change is the essence of narrative.
Keep choppy scene-to-scene jumps without setup when you are portraying the disjointed thought patterns of a distraught or mentally ill character, or stacking scenes like an album of memories.
When you rearrange chronology with flashbacks or out-of-order events, have an important reason: it must serve the piece more than it disrupts.
Hunt out and cut clichéd language—sparkling eyes, jet-black hair, loving someone more than life itself—tired language flattens and kills even exciting scenes.
List every way you could show your character’s desire—through gesture, speech, inner thoughts—and cut any that feel too familiar, stereotypical, or clichéd.
When your story is truly action-based and the action is rising toward a dramatic climax, let fast sections follow on each other’s heels until the climax is reached.
Recast a close-third-person passage in first person (or vice versa) to test the difference in intimacy—close third stays within the perceptions of a single mind.
Consider organizing a creative nonfiction piece nonlinearly, relying on thematic or imagistic organizing principles rather than strict chronology.
Combine interior thoughts, actions, and dialogue in the same scene instead of letting them work in isolation to reveal character.
Find scenes that dramatize information not worth that much space and compress them into summary, so the remaining scenes carry the emphasis.

Compress the spans of time that do not need examination into a single sentence of summary—“Over the next two years Ralph saw his father only a few times”—and save scene for the spans that require careful attention.
Use concrete experience as a ladder to great abstractions, and when the reflection has gone far enough, return to the most precise observations of the world around you.
Check whether your conflicts develop as the piece moves on—intensify and further complicate the initial conflicts rather than leaving them static, and make their resolutions satisfying.
Let conflict reveal character—keep scenes whose only purpose is displaying a trait rare, since too many of them lose the reader.

Decide whether your piece is light entertainment or basically serious with touches of irony, and stay consistent—don’t waver between using characters for humor and expecting readers to be moved by them.
Wield contradiction deliberately: let a character’s words, thoughts, and behavior disagree for effect, but not so much that the character reads as schizophrenic.
Make each turning point grow naturally out of what comes before it—readers won't believe a change that comes out of thin air.
Cut any scene that doesn't ultimately move the piece forward—a scene without conflict must at least serve as setup for conflicts to come.
Cut unnecessary conversations and irrelevant background exposition from your scenes—they slow the pace until the reader loses sight of what’s at stake in the scene.
Cut any summary that explains what a scene has already made obvious; let the scene evoke the most significant events.
Ask the same defining questions of your older, wiser narrator that you asked of the younger self.
Define the differences between your narrator’s older and younger selves: is the younger self naive, hopeful, full of illusions, given to excesses? Pin down its nature.

Find the flat, generic descriptions of your characters—"The old lady sat on the park bench"—and rephrase them with individuating details that reveal nature: coiffure, tailored jacket, expensive shoes.
Name each scene's central desire and the obstacle that thwarts it—desire plus obstacle is what creates narrative tension.
Keep symbolic details concrete and grounded so the symbolism never overwhelms the story—and avoid so many significant details that the scene turns heavy-handed.
Sort your concrete details: a brown dog, a ceramic cup, a hose on the lawn are ordinary unless they carry meaning for the character in this particular scene—make significance count.
Use details to do more than create a believable world: they can carry themes, reveal character, and heighten or provide drama.
Mark the places where you get bored reading your own draft and the holes where it rushes; work out why each drags or races, then cut or add so the narrative moves forward smoothly and compellingly.
Ask yourself whether your use of dialect relies on stereotypes that diminish the humanity of any character—stereotyping only weakens the work.
If you avoid writing dialect, establish each character’s speech habits through word choice and rhythm instead.
Audit each dialogue passage: does it move the scene forward, heighten tension, put forth themes, or reveal character? Cut words or lines that do none of these.
If a passage of dialogue exists only to deliver background, cut it and present that background through narrative summary instead.
When background is carried through dialogue, give it a function in the scene and a reason the character tells that history now.
Make your dialogue seem as though it is generated naturally from the events transpiring, even though you are selecting and shaping it to your own ends.
Check each line of dialogue against its context: when speech doesn't fit the setting and events around the character, that disconnect shows the reader something important about her.
Write dialogue that is natural to the individual: ask what this character would say at that moment, in that circumstance.
Give your dialogue more than one job in the scene—reveal character, tip off region or class, expose themes, heighten drama, provide background—never let it be mere “color.”
Make sure your reader always knows who is speaking: use dialogue tags unless actions and description show the speaker, so no one has to read back.
Infuse your dialogue so it echoes the themes of your piece, the way a character’s talk of mistrust can sound your story’s central note.
Digress in your reflection from the personal to the historical or informational to make the narrative more layered and thought provoking.
Cut any setup summary that pretells something the following scene will show—if the summary reveals what happens, it weakens rather than strengthens the scene.
Before a dramatic scene that is focused on the immediate actions and words of the characters, add setup summary so the reader understands more about the characters than the scene itself can show.
Rewrite events so they are dramatized rather than reported: ground the reader in place and give the illusion of real time passing.
Before lifting your story into big summarized abstractions, supply the specificity of concrete details so the reader trusts you.
Denote a character's emotional state through action or dialogue—a nervous gesture instead of a line that tells us they are nervous.
Choose scene or summary point by point by asking whether you want to engage the reader’s emotions or intellect—there is no formula for how much to show and how much to tell.
Trim your mid-scene summary to only what is needed to convey the character's emotional base and emotional shift, since every interruption of forward movement costs momentum.
Give your characters recognizable yet complex emotions, and render the experience as it happens in time, complete with sensory detail, so the reader goes through it with them.
Check that your piece delivers significant change—in character, narrator, or the reader's perception—by the end of your story, essay, or book.
Shape your ending to leave a sense of closure—if not complete resolution—and ideally to linger in the reader's mind.
Check whether you reached your ending before your final paragraphs—if so, cut off the last paragraph or page or two.
If the ending isn't working, switch scene for summary, try ending earlier or later than you do now, or add a scene or summary to see where it takes you.
Choose an ending built on reflection, epiphany, pointed action, or a haunting sensory detail—each contains a resolution, and don't worry whether it's scene or summary.
Cut the neat-bow wrap-up: an ending that ties off every detail gives closure but won't stay with a reader.
Match the ending's tone and content to everything that came before, whether you cast it in scene or summary.
Create a character using summary: include interior thoughts, external description, summarized behavior, and narrative commentary.
Write a page of summary that condenses thirty years in the history of a family — and make it interesting.
Insert a passage of summary into one of your scenes to deepen the reader's sense of the character.
Write a paragraph of summary in which the narrator establishes a tone of irony, then rewrite the same paragraph shifting the tone to straightforward and pragmatic.

Write two paragraphs of summary with narrative layering: the first in the voice of the narrator as a child, the second in the same narrator’s adult voice — let the older, wiser voice illuminate the younger, more innocent passage.
Practice the scene-summary ratio: write a page where summary dominates and scene appears briefly, then a page where scene dominates and summary appears briefly.
Write a paragraph of summary in the voice of a reflective narrator who has just read an old love letter.
Take a scene you've written and follow it with reflective summary, letting the narrator or character reflect on what just happened.
Select a published scene that contains interspersed summary, remove all the summary embedded in it, and read what remains: what has been lost, and has anything been gained?
Write a few paragraphs of summary that display the use of repeated time.
Write a paragraph of summary about a childhood outing, using vivid sensory detail throughout.
Raise dramatic tension in a scene by opening it with setup summary before the action begins.
Insert a brief expository description into a scene to add texture, symbolism, or a momentary slowing of pace—keep it short enough that it does not interrupt the scene for long.
If your story turns surreal or fantastic, ground it in a seemingly realistic setting first—place the bizarre within the believable so the interplay makes the setting function.
In first-person narrative, notice which details your narrator selects—those choices automatically reveal the narrator’s character.
Keep your reader located in time through every flashback—use time markers on entry and draw attention back to the ongoing action on return, or readers give up.
Drop the announcing verbs from flashback entries—'The last time Dave had run over a squirrel…' functions fine without 'remember' or 'recall' and is less obviously a device.
Include a flashback only when its payoff outweighs the forward momentum it costs, and anchor it to a real connection with the ongoing scene.
Shift the verb tense to mark the move into a flashback—present to past, or a few past-perfect verbs when the scene is already in past tense.
Cut any passage, fast or slow, that does not contribute to the forward movement of the whole.
In revision, keep your language fresh—but don’t hype it to the point where diction and imagery distract from the scene.

Weigh the costs of interrupting your narrative before jumping into the future tense: use it occasionally to telegraph information that will change how the reader judges the current characters and action.

Set your scene-to-summary ratio by genre: in a thriller keep summary to what readers need plus connective tissue between scenes, in romance favor scenes that share the protagonist’s emotions, and in science fiction use exposition to establish the world but scene for the important events.
Plant early references or parallels that foreshadow major events to come—a stumble off a step before a cliff fall—so the momentous scene lands with greater meaning.
In your setup summary, establish the character's routine with markers of repeated time such as “never” and “always” so the scene that follows disturbs a recognizable pattern.
Carve conflict that is less overt: let a character's hidden emotions and motives come through to the reader without stating them.
Do not rush from major plot point to major plot point; let the story pause long enough for the reader to learn something about the human condition along the way.
Express humor through reflective summary—irony, absurdity, exaggeration, odd juxtapositions, sarcasm—where it can’t be voiced in a scene.
When your humor criticizes the reader, include yourself in the criticism—criticize “us,” not “them”—or the reader will feel attacked rather than laugh.
Integrate any inserted history or place description into the overall intention of the story so it echoes the events within the scenes rather than arriving at random.
Before deciding how much scene and summary to use, get clear on what you wish to accomplish in the overall work; your proportions depend on what’s at stake and what you want to emphasize.
Before shaping a character's thoughts, name what you want to accomplish in the scene—then shape the thoughts (or your narrator's) to show exactly what you want them to.
In fiction, use internal monologue to show what lies beneath a character's behavior and appearance—don't waste the opportunity that playwrights and screenwriters don't have.
Try a turning point with no direct confrontation: a character quietly coming to an important decision or seeing the truth about a situation without voicing it.
Check whether your reflective narrator judges the younger self too harshly—heavy judgment can spoil the reader’s experience.
Weigh which narrative voice your scene needs: the limited voice has immediacy, while an older, wiser voice can interpret and comprehend even mid-action.
If your essay is meditative, moving by association rather than plot, let it depend on reflection—a lot of it, as long as it stays relevant and well written.
In memoir or personal essays, choose your details with intention: what you describe reveals what matters to your narrative persona, sets the mood, and hints at themes.
Check that each metaphor and simile makes sense within the context of the scene—the image must fit the material that contains it.
Keep the narrative and your characters primary—technique must serve them, not the other way around.
Vary the intensity of your conflict scenes—if every scene runs at full blast, readers grow exhausted and numb.
Establish mood through concrete details that combine into a tone, rather than naming the mood outright.
Cut any dialogue where a character announces the meaning of the story too directly—characters who serve as mouthpieces for the author lose believability.
Examine the movement in your scene and distinguish physical from emotional movement: does a character change, or does the reader’s perception of the characters change?
In creative nonfiction, make sure your narrator's inner world is on the page and that her thoughts are sufficiently revealing of her character.
To make your narrator sound like a child (or any persona), choose not only the words they would use but also the details they would observe.
Insert summary at a natural pause in the action or dialogue of a scene—such as when a character says something the narrator or protagonist needs to reflect on—rather than mid-momentum.
Don't stack multiple flashbacks in one scene—the backward motion becomes irritating and the interruptions confusing; filter extra memories elsewhere in the story.
If you are writing historical fiction or a period piece, use old-fashioned omniscient narrative reflection to intentionally mimic the style of an earlier time.
Let your intrusive reflective narrator strike a pose of omniscience tempered with self-deprecating modesty.
Open with a brief, vividly rendered scene that hooks the reader, then follow with the background summary—starting with the context loses interest.
If your older narrator feels detached from the younger self, figure out the younger person’s motives—why she was silly or he was cruel—to reconnect the two selves.
Remember that pace comes from time, not form: a scene can be slow because it mimics a deliberate progression of time, and a summary can be rapid because it compresses minutes, days, years.
Where you want distance from events—the narrator telling the story soon or long after it happened—use past tense or past perfect to give both teller and reader breathing room.
If the narrative voice and point of view don’t come naturally, try different versions of the scene and keep the one that best serves your intention.
If your scene needs a moment-by-moment feel—nervous preparations, a ticking countdown—consider present tense.
Where you want events to feel like they are happening in the very moment of narration, write the scene in present tense for immediacy.
When a character receives shocking or confusing information, try present tense to show the character's disjointed response.
Identify the scene at the center of your story—the event everything else spins around, the one that must be returned to—and make sure it is the event you dramatize.
Achieve humorous put-downs through the extremity and absurdity of your examples, but never put down the reader—imply you share the assumptions and the wit.
Insert a quick summary mid-scene—a few summarizing words—that gives the reader a much fuller sense of the characters' situation and shapes the interpretation of the scenes that follow.
Read your dialogue aloud as you work—or have someone read it aloud to you—and rephrase anything that does not sound convincing.
When you follow a scene with reflective summary, make the reflection deepen understanding of the scene or take the reader beyond its events—never restate what the scene has already shown.
Cut any reflection that doesn’t repay the momentum it costs—each reflective passage must add insight or interest for the reader.
Cut a follow-up reflection that is obvious, general, or obscure; keep only what adds something important that engages readers and enlarges the scope of the story.
Rewrite any character reflection that floats in a vague narrative ether so it happens in the moment, inside the scene.
Let your narrative voice tell the reader not just what happened but why it happened or what it means.
After a reflective passage of large abstractions, move quickly into the specifics of your story—don’t build the whole piece from abstractions.
Add reflective summary at points where a distinct narrative voice can ponder and comment on the action or characters.
Write reflection that raises ideas your story will then live out, so the reader is intrigued and hungry to see how the story answers them.
Ask of your dialogue: do the word choices reveal where each character comes from geographically or economically, and what mood they are in?
Check for redundancy between channels: once a character has thought something internally or said it in dialogue, do not repeat it in the other form—once is enough.
Make a resolution scene believable—it must grow naturally out of the characters and actions that precede it and must not feel sentimental, forced, or tacked on.
Match the resolution's scale to the work that precedes it—highly dramatic work earns a dramatic resolution, a small personal story wants a quiet one.
Consider a subtle resolution—the real resolution can be an emotional realization that precedes the story's final, more obvious event.
Build your retrospective story or memoir on the distance between the older, wiser narrator and the younger self as character.
When a character makes a pivotal decision in a scene, insert summary that reveals the process of reasoning behind it—the scene alone shows the choice, not the why.
Make your summaries richly detailed—a summary rendered with rich detail reads as fully dramatized and keeps the story from flattening.
Ask whether you are letting your narrator off the hook: be completely honest in assessing both the younger and older self rather than reflecting in too rosy a light.
Don’t force resolution into every scene: a scene can raise a problem the narrative resolves further along, or introduce themes developed later.
End the scene with a deliberate action—the final position gives that action extra weight.
End the scene on a line of dialogue, cutting off the reply to magnify the final line’s impact and add suspense.
End the scene with an image or lingering action that crystallizes the themes or events of the scene.
End the scene with lingering sensory details that leave the reader with the feeling of the place.
End the scene strongly; don’t let it fizzle out.
Leave a scene unresolved when you want suspense or interest to pull readers into the next scene.
Vary your scene endings—ending every scene with a flourish becomes an obvious device.
Punctuate the scene ending: use it to put form to the scene, emphasize themes, end forward motion, and assert a rest before more scenes and summaries arrive.
When a character makes a choice with dramatic import, recast that moment as a scene rather than a summary.
Open a scene in the midst of action or dialogue when you want to cut to the chase and establish the conflict immediately.
Where your scene moves at a natural pace, limit the description so it doesn't get bogged down—keep only the details that carry a lot of information about the characters.
Manufacture the time that passes in your scene rather than recording it realistically: select only the actions and thoughts that will have the most impact for your intention.
Work the middle of the scene: intensify conflict, develop and reveal character, and move the action forward as complications arise and the stakes rise.
In a piece carried mostly by summary, stop the ongoing flow of summary and render in scene only the moments of utmost importance to your narrator or protagonist.
Check that your scene has movement: by its end the reader should feel in a different place—something changed, or the reader’s perception of the characters changed.
Decide how each scene opens—with a slow buildup from the beginning or in medias res—so the choice fits the subject and the mood you want to convey.
Write plot-critical events as scenes and summarize the routine ones—match the treatment to the event’s importance.
Decide what you need to reveal about the character in this scene, then articulate the scene’s purpose: what the character wants and what obstacles or aid they will encounter.

Check each scene against the jobs scenes perform—emotional connection, dramatized events, plot movement, conflict, suspense, change, character revelation, theme, mood, resolution—and make sure it meets at least a few.
Establish reader interest quickly in the scene’s opening, whether through immediate conflict or an engaging character.
To stretch a moment that took only seconds, heighten the character's perception of physical stimuli—what they feel against their skin, what they hear—and let the language grind to a halt.
Open a scene slowly, with scene-setting description first, when the buildup should set the mood and introduce the theme.
Ask what your adult narrator feels about the younger self in each specific scene—when the younger self was victimized, achieved, or made foolish choices—and let conflicting emotions stand.
To speed a scene up, cut sentences into short subject-action constructions and make the verbs explosive and action-filled.
Check where each scene begins: if you start with every preliminary, cut back to the moment that matters so details and irrelevant events don't bury the reader.
Audit your draft for the balance of scene and summary: good prose needs both, so find where over-scening or over-summarizing weakens the work.
Decide passage by passage whether time should be condensed or expanded: use summary to relay many events quickly, a scene to give the impression of real time passing.
Plant a theme of the larger work early in the scene—even in its first sentence.
Audit each scene for its three structural parts: a way in (beginning), the work it accomplishes (middle), and a graceful exit (ending).
Map the clock inside each of your scenes and take complete awareness and control of it: decide how much time passes and what the reader experiences of it.
Check that each of your scenes is anchored in a specific time and place, with events transpiring in real time.
Match your verbs to your scene's clock: slow verbs where time should crawl, a pile-up of action verbs where time should race.
Keep the scenes and summaries of the younger self’s innocence so the older voice of wisdom has power—show the steps along the way to knowledge.
Consider what second person does to your scene: it either makes the reader the primary character or suggests a narrator estranged from himself—either way it adds tension.
Place yourself inside the scene before writing: expand "see it" to smell, taste, or whatever other sensory details are needed, and describe the setting until it becomes real to you.
Develop the sensory details that pin your character to the moment—a hot puppy's skin, cool air, the tang of coffee—so the fall out of the moment lands dramatically.
Ask what your setting does beyond establishing a believable background: could it carry symbolic meaning, reveal aspects of character, or establish mood and tone?
Compare your scene's setting against the mood you intend: would a change of season, time of day, or state of repair alter the emotional effect on the reader?
Read your setting for what it reveals about character: what would a bedroom tell about its owner—messy or orderly, whose pictures on the dresser?

Elucidate the symbolic weight of any place or object in your scene: it must carry meaning beyond its factual identity, and that meaning must be a part of the narrative—on its own, a crumbling castle is just a crumbling castle.
Before a scene that follows another scene, add a setup summary that provides context or increases dramatic tension so the story flows smoothly instead of jumping choppily.
Don’t let the show-don’t-tell rule silence your narrator—allow a strong reflective voice to ponder and interpret people and events.
Choose similes that advance your themes and set up what’s to come, not merely pleasant images: a lopped-off head sun works because it foreshadows violence.

Locate the abstractions in your work and determine whether each deepens readers’ understanding or makes them turn away: demonstrate big ideas such as love, patriotism, or sacrifice in the particular, moving from the particular to the universal rather than the other way around.
Cut exposition made of details and facts thrown in for their own sake — such as an entire genealogy for a minor character whose family history has no bearing on the central story.

Identify the generalizations in your summaries — blanket statements about ethnicity, gender, age, or education, even generalized praise — and spend time transforming each one into a richly descriptive, individualized portrayal.
Find events in your summaries that require evoking in scene — a moment of revelation or major change in the narrator’s or protagonist’s life — and rewrite them as scenes, not reported summaries.

Where exposition only restates the shown action, replace it with detail that reveals a character oddity — a quirk the scene can't display, like a habit that exposes whether the character is clumsy or self-destructive.

Look over your reflections for grandiose or pedantic comments that set your narrator up as superhumanly wise or benevolent, check the pretentiousness-o-meter, and scale those observations and judgments back down to size.
Cut exposition that merely repeats what your scene already shows or what your dialogue already speaks.

Redline the reflective phrases that have a ring of familiarity — “He loved her with all his heart,” “There is no place like home” — and find a fresh way to get your point across. Push yourself: do you really agree with the familiar line?
Question the necessity of each expository summary: is the information extraneous, or better shown through scenes? Try removing some of your exposition to see if anything has really been lost.
Decide at each point whether scene or summary is called for, and slide between them gracefully.
Slow a scene’s pace by deliberately inserting background summary into the ongoing scene.
Check that every shift from scene to summary feels smooth.
Watch out for characters who make speeches at length, especially with abstractions like courage, honor, or devotion—people rarely make speeches in conversation.
Even a scene in which no one moves from a chair needs emotional movement—a revealing interaction or a shift in the reader’s perception—or it will feel static.
Give a character a detail that breaks their stereotype—the distinguished-looking man video gambling on his laptop—to catch the reader's interest and make them want to know more.
Before using an ironic omniscient reflective narrator, study nineteenth-century omniscient narrators to absorb their diction, syntax, and general style so you can adapt them.
Render a conversation that recurs in repeated time as summarized dialogue—with phrases like “every time” and “then next time”—instead of staging it as a scene.
Load your background summary with a second job — carrying a theme, setting an expectation, building suspense, or starting the story — after articulating your intentions for the piece.
Make each background summary do heavy lifting — it halts the narrative, so cut any that don't earn their place with more than one job.
When your scene can't naturally carry needed background — family history, past events — move that information into summary instead of stuffing it into dialogue or characters' in-scene thoughts.
Keep summarized behavior specific even in general time — select individual characteristics that fit the character and tell who they are, never generic traits.
Characterize obliquely in summary: let the objects and details a person keeps — the car they drive, the foods they prefer — reveal who they are.
Use summary to compress a stretch of time whenever the span of events matters more to the tale than any individual event within it.
Cut from your time-compressing summary every component included only because it happened; compression is selection, and selection gives what remains maximum impact.
Rewrite repeated actions with conditional verbs (would, could) and time adverbs (always, every, sometimes) instead of writing new scenes.
Cut the quickie establishing scene you wrote just to set context; deliver that background in summary instead.
Elaborate a scene with surrounding summary that gives it context, so scene and summary enrich each other.

Before writing a piece of fiction that relies on summary to the near exclusion of scene, consider that very few writers carry it off outside a book-length work; creative nonfiction, with its reliance on reflection, tolerates it better.
Combine exterior and interior in summary: ask your characters what they wear, how they move, where they shop, then tell the answers to reveal how they think generally.

Free write from the character's first-person point of view, even if the piece is third person. Memoirists can free write from their child-self; treat it as a throwaway exercise for entering their interior life.
Summarize the stretch between two scenes — the drive home, the errands, the routine — when none of the intervening events warrants a scene of its own.
Write summary in "general time" for events, information, and ideas not tied to a specific moment — nonscene memories, repeated actions, and reflections that stand alone or sit inside scenes.
To capture a character's irregular thinking in summarized musing, first identify what makes their thinking different, then inhabit the person and let the musings show how the mind works.
Follow up a direct statement of a character's inner state (like "Benna misses everyone") with detailed, habitual evidence, or it reads as a bald assertion.
Describe a place through background summary as part of the piece's overall imaginative landscape — details that exist outside any specific scene and carry your characters' emotional situation.
Cut summaries that run so long the emotional connection is lost, and give readers a breather where scenes pile up.
Indicate repeated time with a list — an array of recurring items (the odd lunches, the things they carried) conveys recurrence without scenes.
Give minor characters backgrounds too — a few carefully selected words that work hard to round them out and enrich the piece.
Test each summary: if it does not deepen themes, reveal character, or express your distinctive voice, it is a distancing shortcut—cut it.
Open with background summary that reveals a character's history and sets the story in motion — even the catalytic event can come in summary rather than a scene.
When an emotion recurs — once is not enough — explore it in summary across a span of time instead of staging it in a single scene.
Tell repeated actions in summary — the recurrence is the point — instead of staging a scene for each occurrence.
Show a repeated behavior through summarized, repetitious dialogue — the litany of a character's recurring complaints — rather than in individual scenes.
Treat summary as the vehicle for information and scene as the vehicle for emotion: give the reader the larger picture in summary, then let the scene carry the visceral experience.
Choose setting details in your summary for what they reveal: pick ones that reflect your characters' emotional states and carry symbolic as well as factual weight.
Establish in background summary the impression of a character that a later scene will contradict and shatter; know that your piece turns on that contrast before setting the expectation.
Get specific when you tell how someone behaves and feels in general — not in time and place, but in detail and emotion — or your summary has no impact.
When your summary leaps across time, keep the reader located with locator tags ("a few months after," "the next week") or details that express time passing.
Find the significant events and moments of change you have only summarized and render them in scene.
Reach past the obvious verbs and adjectives when summarizing a character's habitual behavior; pick the ones that carry the most weight.

Identify the material between your scenes—background exposition, description outside a scene, interior thoughts, repeated events, compressed action, and narrative commentary—and make sure it lives in summary, not scene.
Interrogate a summarized interior statement with Why and How — what does the character actually feel, and how does that feeling show — then extend the summary with your answers.
Rephrase your narrator's descriptions so the verb carries the attitude — "lurking" instead of "hanging around" — every word counts when revealing interior life.
Raise an open-ended question in a scene—if readers are engaged enough to care about the answer, suspense will compel them to read on.
Create suspense by letting the reader know more than the character knows.
Vary your syntax and sentence length: unrelieved subject/verb/object constructions tire the reader, and extremely long convoluted sentences leave them gasping.
Cut adverbs that follow dialogue tags: the action and the words themselves should show the manner of speaking (“Drop dead!” she said angrily is redundant).
Use plain said or says for dialogue tags and cut pointed or whimsical verbs of speech (raged, harrumphed) that distract from the dialogue.
Make sure each dialogue tag is actually a verb of speech—“You’re cute,” she winked makes no sense.
Match your reflective humor to your intent: for entertainment use narrative exaggeration; for literary aims let irony and absurdity shine without overwhelming the story or characters.
Rewrite the same scene in present, past, and future tense and compare: pick the version whose tense matches your intention, whether immediacy, consequences, or a jump from a larger framework.
If you combine tenses in one scene, anchor each jump with time markers so the reader always stays located in time.
Find every random tense switch in your scene—"He went downstairs and reaches for the orange juice"—and either give each switch a reason, an effect you are after, or make the tenses consistent.
Precede a scene with summary that offers relevant information and creates expectation for something important that is about to happen, so the reader is primed before the scene's events unfold.
Remember that not every scene needs conflict, but the piece as a whole must carry narrative tension—without opposition, characters' real natures are never tested or revealed.
Test each summary insertion by making two versions of the scene—one without the insertions and one with them—then add the summary back bit by bit and cut any insertion that adds nothing essential.
Articulate what your story or essay is about on its deepest level—theme, distinct from plot—and make sure the scene emphasizes it.
Check that your time markers haven't gotten so complex or lyrical that they misfire and the reader gets lost.
When you locate a scene in time, let the marker do double duty: instead of stating the facts directly, describe what the narrator sees—a watched sunrise that also establishes setting.
Locate each scene in a specific time with a simple time tag—"June first, 1963", "Last Thursday", "After she went into labor"—whenever the reader needs an anchor.
Move from scene to summary or scene to scene by carrying an associative link—a word, image, or sensory detail—across the shift.
Keep readers oriented by maintaining a straightforward chronology, and mark flashbacks clearly whenever you jump backward in time.
Cut excessive cliff-hanger juxtapositions—too many and the device becomes obvious and tiresome.
When you leave a scene for summary, add a connecting phrase that links logically and chronologically to what just happened in the scene.
Pivot from scene into summary through an image that carries psychological weight: let the character's eye land on an object in the scene that triggers her reflection.
Set one scene or summary against another so the juxtaposition itself forms the transition, for ironic or emotional effect.
If your narrative is nonlinear, keep readers oriented by providing dates at the headings of each chapter.
Use a white space break on the page to mark a shift in time, place, or narrative mode between scenes and summaries—or even a chapter break.
When you come out of a summary into a scene, open with an indicator of time—like 'The following Saturday…'—so readers know exactly when and where they are.
If your scenes and summaries are short, cut back on space breaks and find other forms of transition, so your pages don't read like a list of vignettes.
Render turning points in the action or a character's emotions as scenes, never as summary.

Rewrite the setup so the character's habitual, ordinary behavior is established in summary, then break that habit in a scene where the character steps out of the summarized behavior—that break is your turning point.
Before a scene, raise an unanswered question in the setup summary—relevant detail that creates an expectation in the reader—to build tension for what follows.
Choose verbs for their emotional associations: he croaked versus he expired both mean dead, but each carries the narrator’s attitude and sets the tone.
Write your summaries as narrative commentary in your own distinctive voice—voice often comes through best there.
Withhold a key fact from your reflective summary, dropping hints along the way, so the reveal lands with playful surprise in straightforward language.
Define the younger self’s situation in terms of geography, housing, family, school, and work.

Go through a passage of your own prose and find every adverb whose meaning the verb already carries, and every adjective whose meaning the noun already carries. Rewrite so the verb or noun itself does the work.
Scan a page of your own writing and list the qualifiers you reach for again and again — your habitual 'very', 'just', 'kind of'. Cut every one that is not earning its place.
Find every 'somehow' in your draft and replace it with the actual cause or mechanism. Nothing can happen somehow.
In your adjective-free, adverb-free passage, allow only the time adverbs that are genuinely necessary — then, next, later — and keep even those to a minimum.
Write your first adjective-free, adverb-free draft on new material, not on something you've already written. Save your old passages for later rounds of the exercise.

Reread your adjective-free passage and ask: would adding an adjective or adverb here and there improve it, or is it satisfactory without? Keep it chaste unless a specific qualifier earns its way back in.

Look back at your adjective-free draft and notice the devices and usages the constraint forced you into — especially your choice of verbs and your use of simile and metaphor. Name what changed in your writing.
Repeat your descriptive scene in the voice of a character instead of the authorial voice — let a character in the story describe it.
Apply Chekhov's Razor to your draft: throw out the first three pages — starting a story, we all circle around, explain a lot of stuff, and set things up that don't need to be set up.
Put two people into a crisis situation — the car out of gas, the spaceship about to crash — and let their talk carry the story.
In your first draft crowd in everything boldly; then in revising decide what counts and what tells, and cut and recombine till what is left is what counts.

Audit what you crowd in and where you leap: everything crowded in to enrich the story sensually, intellectually, emotionally should be in focus, part of the story's center, and every leap should follow the trajectory of the whole.

Check each paragraph of your story for slackness: keep the story full of what is happening in it, moving, not wandering into irrelevancies, and interconnected with itself, rich with echoes forward and backward.
Find the flabby phrases and cliches in your draft and replace them with the vivid phrase, the exact word: never use ten vague words where two will do.
Expect severe cutting to include some of your favorite, most beautiful and admirable sentences and passages, and cut them anyway; you are allowed to cry or moan while you do.
In revision, cut any passage that sticks out or leaves the main trajectory; notice how often a cut that seemed sure to leave a terrible hole joins up without a seam.
Write a scene as pure dialogue — no stage directions, no description of the characters — so everything the reader knows comes through what the characters say.
Practice psychological displacement: write a scene from inside a person of a different gender, age, or generation, even though it feels hard and scary.
Cut every detail that doesn't tell: a mere inventory of articles bores the reader — make each detail build the mood you want.
Find where your narrative pours out information as a lecture and break up the Expository Lump — grind the information into the story instead.
Find the chunk of background information in your scene and compost it: break it up, spread it out, and slip it into conversation or action-narration as implication, passing reference, or hint.
Rewrite your scene so the process runs with at least two people present, either in the background of a conversation or as the locus of the action.
Choose something you know how to do that involves a complex series of specific actions — making bread, sailing a boat, repairing an engine — and build a scene around the process.
Make your scene understandable to a reader who has not read your background notes: include enough of the situation that it stands alone without them.
Make the steps of the process clear to the reader, but keep it in the background — the process should not appear to be what the piece is about.
Learn to read your own work as a reader: you and you alone can judge it, and the judgment can be made rightly only by a writer who has learned to read her own work.

Put a finished piece away and forbid yourself to look at it for at least a week, then reread it with a friendly critical eye, with revision in mind: to see its faults and virtues you need to look at it after a real interval.
Read your finished piece aloud to yourself: speaking and hearing it will show up awkward bits and faults in the rhythm, and can help you make the dialogue natural and lively.
Reread your piece looking for what is awkward, unclear, excessive, and what breaks the pace or does not work — then cut or fix it.
Develop your craft deliberately: skill in writing frees you to write what you want to write, and it may also show you what you want to write.
Do not wait on luck: you can learn skill, you can earn it, and you can learn to deserve your gift.
Write each scene as the account of an act or action, not a static scene: make something happen, so it ends up in a different place from where it started.
Write to a short, set length and do not exceed it: the limit is itself excellent discipline.
Write a paragraph seriously in the style of a writer you admire, not as parody or pastiche: imitation done seriously is a demanding and revealing exercise.
Read masterful books attentively, with a consciousness of technique in mind: it is useful as well as enjoyable.
Practice invisible exposition: tell the reader things without appearing to tell — let the information ride inside the story.
Read your action scenes — a fist-fight, a battle, a sports event — for blow-by-blow accounts, which create confusion and boredom; leap instead, fast enough and far enough.
In an action passage, include everything the reader needs to know and nothing more; make the sensory details intense, brief, and precise, and the language transparent.
Look at what you can leave out of your prose: what you leave out is infinitely more than what you leave in, so leave white space around the word, silence around the voice.
Leap over years at a time in your narrative, omitting great wads of the protagonist's life; omit the explanations and let the connections make themselves.
Find any description where you tried to include everything and cut it down: overcrowded descriptions clog the story and suffocate themselves.
Write from inside your story character: tell only what that single character perceives, feels, knows, remembers, and guesses.

Cut anything in your limited-third-person scene that the viewpoint character cannot perceive — if Della wouldn't see her own violet eyes, don't describe them; if she is aware of them, show it through her action.
Let a character talk through you: be quiet, listen, and write what they think and say as it rises from inside them.
Cut the expository freight from your memoir — the load of explaining and describing can stall it just as badly as it stalls science fiction.
Let the people in your memoir speak in their own voices — if everyone says only what you wanted to hear, all we hear is an interminable monologue.
Revive a memory of someone you disliked or held in contempt and write the moment from that person's point of view, guessing how they felt, what they saw, and how they perceived you.
Test every line of dialogue against how people actually talk, and rework anything that sounds stagey.

Write a sketch of an old woman at a present activity — washing dishes, gardening, whatever — as she thinks about an event from her youth, intercutting between "now" and "then" with at least two time-jumps.
Write the sketch in a chosen person (first or third) and a chosen tense arrangement — all past, all present, "now" present with "then" past, or "now" past with "then" present — and label your choice.
Now write the same story again in the other person and a different choice of tenses, and label it.
When you write the second version, don't find-replace the pronouns and verb endings on a computer — write it over, and let the changed person and tense change the wording.
Within one version, keep the person of the verb constant — only the tense may shift.
Compare your two versions: which pronoun works best for the story, which tense suits the material, how awkward are the time-shifts, and what actually differs between the versions?
Read narrative prose with a particular consciousness of what persons and tenses of the verb are used, why the author used them, and how often the narrative tense changes.
Find the passive constructions in your prose, name the doer, and make the doer the subject — convert them to active voice.
Scan your prose for passives used because they are indirect and polite; rewrite them so someone takes responsibility — who thought it, who did it.
Check that the passive hasn't seeded itself into your style where it doesn't belong, and root it out.
Before banning the passive voice, know what it is: the passive is not the verb to be.
Use the past tense for easy movement in time: it gives access to times before and after the period of the narrative and implies continuity.
In past-tense narration, use the past perfect for a time before the narrative moment — "I hadn't seen," not "I didn't see."
Look at your story apart from its plot — plot merely connects happenings in causal chains and is not superior to story, and not even necessary to it; some great stories have neither.
Tell the story of an accident twice: once in the detached author mode or in a journalistic, reportorial voice, then from the viewpoint of a character involved in the accident.
Add a character who was there but not a participant, only an onlooker, and tell the same story in that character's voice.
If a story sticks and won't go right, try changing who tells it: the choice of point of view makes an immense difference to the tone, the effect, even the meaning of the story.
For every shift of viewpoint character in your story, be aware of it, have a reason for it, and stay in control of it.
Retell your scene in the detached-author voice: say only what a neutral observer (a fly on the wall) could infer from behavior and speech, and never enter a character's mind.
Clarify that the "I" or third-person narrator of your fiction is not you, and decide how reliable that narrator is — unreliable narrators may deliberately or innocently misrepresent the facts.

Cut anything in your first-person scene that the viewpoint character could not know, feel, perceive, think, guess, or remember — the reader infers other people only from what "I" sees and says of them.
Don't default to your genre's conventional POV: for romance, first person, observer-narrator, and involved author narration are equally suited to the genre.

Hunt out inconsistent or frequent POV shifts in your story: unless handled with awareness and skill, they jerk the reader around, bouncing between incompatible identifications, confusing emotion, and garbling the story.
When you expand a scene into the involved-author voice, give the story a context: find out what led up to it, and follow it further.

In an involved-author passage, let the narrative shift freely among characters' perceptions and into analysis or prediction only the author could make — a description of a room with nobody there to see it.
Understand your default to limited third person: it became the predominant modern fictional voice partly in reaction to the Victorian fondness for involved author narration and its abuses.

Check your limited-third-person scene: nothing may be seen, known, or told except what the viewpoint character sees, knows, and tells — this limitation concentrates the voice and gives it authenticity.

If you're a memoirist, practice limited third person by inventing a story with made-up characters — using it on factual narrative is trespassing, since you can't know what another real person thought and felt.
In your memoir, flag any narration of another real person's private thoughts or motives as your guesswork, opinion, or interpretation — a memoirist can't be omniscient, even for a moment.
In your POV practice scenes, use little or no dialogue: while characters talk, their voices cover the POV, and you're not exploring that voice.

When you move a passage from first to limited third person, don't just switch the pronoun and verb endings: treat it as a change of voice, because the reader's relationship to "I" is not the same as to "he" or "she".
If you use an observer-narrator, keep them a witness rather than the protagonist: the story is about events they witnessed, not about them.
In your memoir or nonfiction narrative, remember that the "I" is the author: hold yourself to relating what happened, and don't change facts to make the story neater.
Retell the same story from the point of view of one of the other people involved in it.
Treat any POV shift as a major change of voice: going from first to third person, or from involved author to observer-narrator, affects the whole tone and structure of your narrative.
For your involved-author practice, choose a story that concerns you, not one you use to preach.
Present a character's unspoken thoughts directly, exactly as you would dialogue, but without quotation marks or italics — just make it clear the thought is going on inside someone's head.
Don't attempt quick, unsignalled POV shifting unless you command it with immense certainty and skill — it dissolves viewpoints into one another and is rare for a reason.
When you shift point of view, check that you know when and how you are doing it, so that the reader is carried effortlessly with you.
If you shift between first and third person in a short piece, ask whether you have a compelling reason for it — this shift is enormously difficult at that length.
Check your piece for a shift between a detached and an involved authorial voice — you cannot mix the two modes within one piece.
Where your narration moves from one viewpoint character to another often, tighten control until the reader is never jerked from mind to mind or unsure whose mind they are in.
Find any momentary slip into another character's viewpoint — even a single word of what they see or feel — and cut it.
Where you want distance, narrate in third person from the involved author's position, freely limiting perception to a single character for a while.
Rewrite your scene shifting among several viewpoint characters in limited third person, marking each change with a line break or the narrator's name.
Rewrite your scene shifting point of view from character to character several times, deliberately, with no obvious signal to the reader that you are doing so.
Consciously and deliberately imitate a piece of prose you admire, as training toward finding your own narrative voice — the consciousness is what matters.
As the involved author, you may dip into another character's viewpoint for a single moment — do it with care, and never in limited third person.
Recognize that involved-author narration and limited third person overlap: with a subtle authorial voice, it can be hard to tell which mode a piece is written in.
Recognize that fear of plagiarizing and an individualistic valuation of originality can stop you from using deliberate imitation as a learning tool.
Know that in the present tense narration is linear, leading moment to next moment and excluding global temporal reference — it implies discontinuity.
If you write in the present tense, keep out simple and compound past forms and the future — they become awkward and highly artificial.
Don't mistake a narrow focus for immediacy — the present tense's narrow focus merely leaves out more.
Be aware that the present tense flattens the affect of your voice and produces a curious sameness in narrative.
In present-tense narrative, write "then," not "now" — this is a story, not actuality.
Name the punctuation marks you avoid out of fear or uncertainty. Practice using them until they feel like tools in your kit, not rules to trip you.
Go through a draft and mark every place you used language carelessly or stupidly. Rewrite those sentences, because language misused breeds lies and half-truths even with the best intentions.
Treat using language well as your first duty as a writer. For each sentence you write, ask whether your use of language is honest.
Before you 'correct' a sentence, ask whether the rule serves clarity or just marks you as a member of a grammatical in-group. Do not let correctness become a shibboleth that divides writers.
Scan your written prose for incorrect usage that is not part of a conscious, consistent dialect voice. Rewrite it, because left alone it can invalidate the whole piece.
Find the half-finished sentences and misused words in your writing that would pass aloud but fail on the page. Rewrite them so the words alone are clear, without voice or intonation to help.
Find a place where you broke a grammar or punctuation rule. Rephrase the sentence so the break reads as a knowing choice, not an error — you may only break the rules you know.
Scan your prose for ungrammatical, overcorrected, or colloquial usages that stick out on the page. Cut them — they make the sentence sound all wrong even when they are not morally wrong.
List the punctuation problems you have with your own writing: what you feel uncertain about, and which rules you are impatient with — those are the places where your prose will slip.
Look up every punctuation usage that worries you. Study model examples from writers you trust and practice imitating them until the usage feels easy.

Take a few paragraphs of prose you admire and study the punctuation in them: why did the author break that sentence there, where did she want a pause, how much of the rhythm is carried by the punctuation?

Rewrite a passage of your own narrative with all punctuation removed — no paragraphs, no breaks — so it must make itself clear without punctuation. Then punctuate it again, rewriting wherever the punctuation was doing the work, and ask which version is stronger.
Read through a draft for sentences where a missing or misplaced comma changes the meaning. Make sure each comma commits the sentence to what you actually mean.
Find the movement in your story's quietest moments: a letter sent that doesn't arrive, a thought unspoken, the passage of a summer — that can be action enough.
Read your writing out loud — not in a whisper — and hear how natural or stagey it sounds, where the emphasis goes wrong.
Repeat a small, quiet description word for word later in the story, so the changed context gives it a different, deeper resonance.
Find a spot where you swapped a repeated word for a farfetched thesaurus substitute; keep the honest repetition instead.
Scan your draft for a word repeated without carrying emphasis; fix it with a synonym or a different phrasing.
Find a paragraph where you avoided repeating a word out of rule, and let the repetition back in.
Inventory the repetition in your story beyond single words: repeated phrases, images, the word 'said', near-repetition of events, echoes, reflections, variations.
Find where your prose repeats a beat as obviously as poetry's rhyme and chime, and revise so the sameness is subtler.
Hunt out the repetition that gives your prose its rhythm — it works hidden and obscure, not obvious.
Rewrite a passage with open, fearless repetition and read it aloud; let the repeated words carry their due majesty and power.
Write a passage meant to be read aloud that uses repetition as incantation — as a structural device and for laughter.
Give a character a catchphrase and repeat it, verbatim or nearly so, throughout the story; the reader will wait for it and it will grow funny.
Notice how each return of a repeated phrase gathers weight; let the darkness underneath the funniness grow darker with every repetition.
Map the happenings in your story and find the events that echo one another.
Reread your opening chapter and list the images and themes it plants that the rest of the book repeats, with variations.
Rewrite a paragraph of narrative (about 150 words) so a noticeable noun, verb, or adjective appears at least three times — not an invisible word like 'said' or 'was'.
Elaborate a paragraph to a page of narrative (200-400 words) in which one syntactical construction, or one exact rhythm, repeats several times.
Connect two sentences that share an exact rhythm with a one-word swing like 'But'.
If you can't hear that two sentences share a rhythm, say them aloud — chant them — until you hear the sameness.
Treat exact syntactic repetition as an exercise in awareness, not as a technique to leave in finished story prose.
Carry exact repetition only as far as you can before the prose goes monotonous; check and revise against the monotony as you write.
Write a short narrative (350-1000 words) in which something said or done is later echoed or repeated — in a different context, by different people, or on a different scale.
When critiquing, concentrate on the effectiveness of the repetitions and whether they are obvious or subtle.
In memoir and nonfiction, beware forcing unlike events into a repetitive pattern — it distorts the events of a life.
Collect examples of structural repetition from fiction and nonfiction you admire; noticing how repetition and echoing build structure will sharpen your appreciation.
Treat revision consciously as a time to consider what could go out if it had to: cut repetitions, unnecessary explanations, and everything that merely pads.
In your description, reach for senses other than sight — sound above all, and a particular scent or stink that sets the feeling-tone.
Rewrite your scene so each sentence leads to the next until the scene ends.
Treat sentence length as a rhythm instrument: as you revise, consider how the length of each sentence beats the pace of your prose.
Vary your sentence lengths: a page of all-short sentences sounds stupid, a page of all-long ones sounds stuffy.
Match each sentence's length to what it says and does: let a complicated perception or feeling work itself out in a long sentence, and keep a simple action in a short one.
Write a long sentence so its length gives weight to the last clause; read it aloud to hear where the weight falls.
Find two sentences you would normally separate with a period and rephrase them as one sentence joined by a semicolon, so the connection between them stays visible and the flow continues.
Build sentences more deliberately than you speak them: because you can revise, you are not bound to speech-like short prose.
Write a half-page to a page of narrative, up to 350 words, that is all one sentence.
Write a paragraph of narrative, 100 to 150 words, in sentences of seven or fewer words; no fragments — every sentence must have a subject and a verb.
Use a very long sentence when powerful, gathering emotion is building, or when you want to sweep a lot of characters in together.
Elucidate any long sentence whose syntax could lose the reader; make the syntax clear and assured so no one has to go back and start over.

Cut the mechanical rule that sentences and paragraphs must be kept short: it comes from journalism, not from good prose, so let the story, not the rule, decide where your sentences and paragraphs break.
Tell the same story twice, once in short sentences and once in long ones, and see what the sentence length does to the story.
Don't read "show, don't tell" as listing actions and objects without interpreting — keep your judgment and emotion in the text.
Hear your prose as sound before meaning: the basic elements of language are physical — the noise words make and the rhythm of their relation.
Cultivate an awareness of what your own writing sounds like — it is an essential skill for a writer, and one you can relearn.
Train your mind's ear: readers hear the sound of your prose even when they read in silence, so listen to your own writing the way they do.
Listen for the faults in the sound of your prose — dull, droning, jerky, feeble — and cut them. Keep what is lively, well-paced, flowing, strong, and beautiful.
Make each narrative sentence lead to the next — that is its chief duty, keeping the story going.
Read your writing aloud, and loudly — that is how you hear what your prose sounds like.
You have to hear your writing to feel its rhythm — pace and movement depend above all on rhythm.
Gorgeousness is not one style: there are lots of ways to be gorgeous, so find the way that fits your own prose instead of imitating one model.
Write with exuberant vocabulary and musical, dramatic phrasing — give your readers a lifelong sense of the pure beauty of language.
Choose your characters' names for their sound: names are under the fiction writer's control.

Write a paragraph to a page (150-300 words) of narrative that's meant to be read aloud, using onomatopoeia, alliteration, repetition, rhythmic effects, made-up words or names, dialect — any sound effect you like. Don't use rhyme or regular meter: this is a prose exercise.
Rewrite your scene so that what happens happens in the sounds of the words and the rhythms of the sentences — let the events take place in the sound itself.
Reframe your read-aloud piece as one written for children, if that's the only way you can give yourself permission to cut loose and play with sound.
Take the view out the window, the mess on the desk, or something weird somebody said, and make a gorgeous sentence or two or three out of it.
Take your sound piece and play some more with it — improve it here and there, make the sound of it still stronger and livelier.
Ask yourself whether concentrating on the sound of your writing released or enabled anything unusual or surprising — a voice you haven't often used.
Describe the stage without the actors on it: say nothing directly about the absent person or untold event that is the real subject — let the place suggest it.
Start a story from just a character, a conversation, a situation, or a place — no elaborate plot plan needed — and find the story there.
Check whether you have conflated story with conflict: conflict is one kind of behavior; a complex narrative needs the others too — relating, finding, bearing, losing, discovering, parting, changing.
Test your story against the definition: a narrative of events, external or psychological, which moves through time or implies the passage of time, and which involves change. Where is the change?
State your story's focus — what it is about, who it is about: the explicit or implicit center to which all the events, characters, sayings, and doings refer.
Check whether your story can be retold as a plot without fatal loss: if the story is not in the plot but in the telling, make sure the telling, not the plot summary, carries it.
If you are a beginning writer, consider building your narrative on the armature of a strong, shapely plot: a pleasure in itself, reusable generation after generation.
Trace your story's trajectory: the movement — straight ahead, roundabout, recurrent, or eccentric — which never ceases, from which no passage departs entirely, and to which all passages contribute.
Where your scene is nothing but voices, create the story-world and its people around the dialogue — with only disembodied voices, too much is missing.
Choose a viewpoint character you can actually write inside: someone profoundly different from you socially, culturally, or by language or nation may not be accessible to you as a character.
Write from inside a viewpoint character you dislike, suspending judgment — walk a mile in their moccasins and see the world through their eyes instead of exposing how awful they are.
Get yourself, your ego, your opinions, your mental junk out of the way: find the focus of the story and follow the movement of the story, and let the story tell itself.
Remember that in narrative, the past tense is not past and the present tense is not present — both are entirely fictive.
Write abstract discourse and generalities in the present tense — generalities aren't time-bound.
Don't write present-tense generalities about people or practices that belong to the past — describe what is past as past.
Practice the past tenses you're hesitant about until they come freely — regaining free use of them increases your range of options as a storyteller.
Signal every switch of narrative tense with a line break, a dingbat, or a new chapter — otherwise your reader gets mixed up about what happened before what.
Before changing tenses mid-story, ask yourself whether you have a reason for the change — a tense switch is a big deal, like changing viewpoint characters.
Take a piece of narrative prose you have written, 400-1000 words, and cut it by half: count the words, reduce them to half that many, and keep the narrative clear and the sensory impact vivid.
If your piece has dialogue, cut every long speech and conversation in half just as implacably as you cut the narration.
After severe cutting, weigh your words and name which proved to be styrofoam and which gold: severe cutting intensifies your style, forcing you both to crowd and to leap.

Rewrite your There-is and There-are constructions with exact, colorful verbs — "Three great oaks stand on the road to Doomthorpe" is stronger than "There are three great oaks on the road to Doomthorpe."
Don't ban the There-is construction outright — it is not inherently wrong and has its uses in the right place.
Give a glimpse of an event's mood and nature by describing the place where it happened or is about to happen — never the event itself.
Differentiate each character's voice until a reader could tell the speakers apart without name tags.
Create and explain the world of your story inside the story itself — the reader has no way to know it unless the narrative tells them.
Compress your poem to austerity — strip every word that does not earn its place, since poetry usually involves austere compression.
Fix the major problems in your manuscript before starting a page-by-page, front-to-back revision, so you don’t grow cold on the work.
Check whether your article builds toward a climax instead of making one point after another on a plateau.
Search your draft for a buried anecdote that could be made stronger than your present opening, and consider promoting it to the top.
Hunt for the moments in your draft that could produce ten seconds of boredom — an audience has almost no tolerance for a mishap — and cut them.
Treat everything in your writing as calculated for effect — every word and its order chosen deliberately, the way Lincoln calculated almost everything for effect.
