Edit each sentence against the two objectives of all prose — clarity and precision — and rework anything that fails either.
Write at the same time every day and re-revise without balking — set aside the excuses, since difficulties do not excuse the work.
Take a story you admire and dissect it over and over — read it repeatedly until it surrenders the secrets of how it works.
Rewrite the dry passages of your draft so they enable the reader to see as they read, move them, and stimulate the intellect with insight — otherwise the writing fails its purpose.
Rephrase the passage so it evokes an emotion in the reader rather than merely communicating how you feel — the emotional effect is better suited to your purpose.
Practice consciously providing an extraordinary experience for the reader — craft so the reader is oblivious to the fact that they are seeing words on paper.

Remove raw information from your fiction: when information obtrudes, the experience of the story pauses and the author seems to be filling in — cut anything that distracts from the experience even momentarily.
Elaborate your report by setting what you saw in a framework — what has happened elsewhere or in the past — so the scrim lifts, sight becomes insight, and reporting becomes art.
Find the flat, cliché-ridden phrases in your draft and rewrite them with fresh simile and metaphor — the electricity of fresh imagery empowers the reader’s feelings and compels attention.

Check the intention behind your draft: if it is self-expression, a message, or being liked by readers, reset it so your purpose is providing the reader an experience superior to what they encounter in everyday life.
Have a friend with no talent for acting read your draft aloud in a flat monotone, as if the words had no meaning; wherever the emotion dies, rewrite so the words themselves carry it.
Find the raw, pedestrian facts in your nonfiction and elaborate them with images, anecdotes, characterization, and writerly precision — borrow fiction’s techniques to bring the page alive.
Audit your nonfiction for invention: you may make readers feel what happened, but you dare not invent what happened, cannot invent actions, and cannot guess what people were thinking.
Rewrite your opening so it arouses curiosity instead of answering everything up front — a reader who is sated by the first paragraph moves on to the next story.
Before writing each scene, plan the reader’s adventure through it; after a respite away from it, revise with an editor’s steel gaze to see how the reader’s experience might be improved.
Practice your craft deliberately, as ballet dancers, pianists, and actors do — only writers expect to achieve mastery without practice.
Make the writing a good experience for both partners — you and the reader — and stop ignoring the reader’s pleasure in the exchange.
Scan your draft for sameness — the same sentence shapes and rhythms, like a blue suit with a blue shirt and blue tie — and rewrite for variety.
Rewrite the passage so it evokes sensation in the reader — not the fact that it’s raining, but the feeling of being rained upon.
Take a statistic in your draft and refocus it on one individual the reader can see — lose the numbers and focus on the person, as 1,400 homeless people become the man on the 88th Street bench.
Read a few chapters of a transient bestseller and study its mistakes — you can learn more from the painfully bad than from masterpieces, and it sharpens your editorial eye.
Treat expert criticism as something to endure and perfect against: no matter how advanced your career, criticism cuts to the quick, so keep working to challenge it.
Take an incident you witnessed or remember and write not what happened but what might have happened — let it be a taking-off point, not a report.
Check that your work does its job with you absent — the writing alone must act on the reader’s mind and emotions, because the writer is dispensable and the work must do the job.
Find what your characters see or sense in silence but never say, and write the words that reveal what would otherwise be blinked away.
Characterize your protagonist through action in the opening, set up the conflict, and involve the reader in the character's emotional state.
Introduce action into your first sentence — guards rushing to the scene — to help dramatize it.
Use your first sentence to announce your theme dramatically — 'The two most successful creations of American movies are the gangster and the Westerner: men with guns.'
Convey a person's attitude through a visual detail instead of the cliché — show the head held high rather than saying he was 'maintaining his innocence.'
Search your draft for a good lead buried elsewhere and bring it forward to replace a less worthy beginning, so the reader is turned on to reading the whole.
Open with candor — something you would rather the world not know, that you might keep secret if you were not a writer.
Make the character you open with quickly more interesting than most of the people who surround us in life, so the reader becomes involved in that life rather than merely savoring your language.
Give the character in your first scene something he wants badly, and let the reader feel it early — we are immediately interested in a character who wants something badly.
Open with characterization — a personality trait or predicament — instead of incident, and let it seize the reader's attention on its own.
Find a detail in your first sentence whose description clashes with what happens — a deadly bridge called 'the finest' — so the reader wants to know what happened and why.
Pack your first paragraph with concrete detail while introducing the main characters and the tension between them.
Replace flat intensifiers with a concrete, original metaphor that conveys degree — 'pain without pity or horizon' rather than 'endless' — and let contrast sharpen it.
Enhance the hard fact in your opening with contrast, resonance, and surprise — 'In death, life.'
Choose the word that identifies your lead subject by what creates contrast with the event — 'grandmother' rather than her name — to make the difference work.

Pair a shocking desire with a countervailing force that complicates it — the repugnance of having to touch the person you want to strangle — so the reader feels the tension rather than just the shock.
Reframe a flat factual lead to turn on the engine of curiosity — find the surprising measure in it, like the family that took fourteen years to move two blocks.
Cut the abstractions from your opening — a version bloated with abstractions is boring to read no matter how accurate.
Stop cramming who, what, when, where, and why into your first paragraph — naked facts are not enough to invite the reader into the rest of the story.
Cut any opening that describes a happy, harmonious, conflict-free state — 'a wonderful couple' who never argued — the worst possible way to start a story.
Cut the melodramatic, clichéd phrases from your account — a head dropping 'like a rock,' a back heaving convulsively — they turn the writing unbelievable.
Check your lead for straining-for-effect analogies and cut the ones where the reader can feel you trying too hard to lure him into dull material.
Open your piece with a surprising image and hold back the subject's identity for a delayed reveal — 'several hundred bearers of a strategic commodity... They are goats.'
Study the first few pages of the books that have pleased you most and locate the exact place where the engine turns on — where you could not put the book down.
Find the point at which the reader makes the decision not to put the book down — the engine — and move it as close to the top of page one as you can.
Let metaphor and colorful exaggeration enliven your opening sentences to tempt the reader on, so long as the excess does not mislead anyone about what happened.
Move your most interesting fact from the first sentence to the last of the opening paragraph, where it thrusts the reader forward into the next paragraph and establishes tone.
Craft your nonfiction facts so they touch the reader's emotions — information sticks best when it is crafted that way.
Make your first sentence deliver several facts at once, each of which raises a question the reader wants answered — age, situation, regularity, and the interruption to come.

Ask of your first sentence: does it convey an interesting personality or an action we want to know more about, and can it be made more intriguing by introducing something unusual, shocking, or surprising?
Revise your first three pages so they arouse the reader's interest enough to quarantine him from distraction for the several hours the book demands from him.
Find the one word in your opening that characterizes your character in a flash — 'ferret' — and make sure that word is doing the work.
Check your opening: does it immerse the reader in heightened experience, emotional or intellectual, more rewarding than the life around him, or does it bore him toward the death end of the line?
Invert a familiar phrase in your first sentence — 'Saints should always be judged guilty until they are proved innocent' — to produce two attention-getters in half a sentence.

Run your draft first paragraph through the checklist: does the first sentence trigger curiosity, what will the reader see in it, have you focused on an individual with a visible characteristic doing or saying something, and is there a startling or odd fact that will trap attention?
End an ominous sentence with a run of short, monosyllabic words to strengthen the feeling, as in 'the next snow fell.'
Position your narrator in a relationship to the main character that itself raises questions the reader wants answered — will he keep putting up with this person, will the person get what he is after?
Treat your nonfiction opening with the same goal as a fiction writer: spark the reader's interest sufficiently to engage him in reading the rest.
Mint a novel comparison for a familiar object — four giant Oscars 'like sullen art deco Nazis' — and trim the hedging that weakens it.
Instead of a loud hook, seduce the reader leisurely by planting omens that something is going to happen, building apprehension before the action starts.

Check your opening paragraph against the three goals: does it excite the reader's curiosity about a character or a relationship, introduce a setting, and lend resonance to the story? Revise until the first is strongly at work.
Replace the flat, abstract name for a character trait with an original, concrete word — 'thirsty' instead of 'ambitious.'
Try opening with pseudo-candor — a disclaimer that does the opposite of what the reader expects and is a cover-up for a fault — as effective as candor.
Try a quiet first sentence that intrigues through implication rather than shock — 'She might have been waiting for her lover.'
Repeat a key word in your lead to underscore the detail that matters — repetition for effect increases the dramatic impact of what's being described.
Start with a scene the reader can see, and begin that scene as close to its climax as is feasible to involve the reader quickly.
Keep a conventional opening if you like, but season it with just enough that is unconventional to rouse the reader's curiosity — a narrator who is 'naked at the moment and talking into the dark.'
Open with an injunction of secrecy or a promise of revelation — 'You must not tell anyone what I am about to tell you' — that makes the reader want what is being withheld.
Give your subject a small observed action — ducking his head — to picture him, the way a novelist would.
Introduce sound into your lead — the meeting room 'to loud applause' — to make it better.
Open by spotlighting a single individual, characterized however briefly, performing an eccentric and somehow beautiful act — an excellent way of involving the reader's emotions.
Plant an early surprise that unsettles the reader's expectation — a twist on who the speaker is or on what you led them to assume.
Pair an unexpected subject with an unexpected attitude in your first sentence — 'I have long been an admirer of the octopus' — to be both surprising and a touch amusing.
Introduce a visual element into your lead — a head held high, trouble keeping his eyes on the judge — to perk it up.
Open with a visual parallel that connects two incongruous elements — the mourners in scuffed white sneakers at the viewing of a draftsman of shoes.
Present your narrator's core problem through a concrete visual image rather than an abstract statement of it — show the wrong parents, don't say 'I was born to the wrong parents.'
Check your action sequences: anything that is mere motion, things merely happening, replace with action, which is what people do and say.
Re-read your scene for the sound of your own voice and cut it: direct what happens onstage, but never appear as one of the actors.
Elaborate your static descriptions so each one does more than one job: a setting that also reveals the narrator's state of mind, a room that characterizes the person who lives in it.
Rewrite flat exchanges as adversarial dialogue: combative words between characters excite readers' emotions more than sword-play.
Test each scene of your piece: could a camera film it? If a scene cannot be filmed, it is not immediate — rework it until it happens visibly before the reader.
Find the places where you tell offstage events in summary, and rewrite them as immediate scenes the reader witnesses firsthand.
Wherever your scene needs information, find a way to have it come naturally out of the characters in the scene instead of stating it baldly in your own voice.
Cut the transitions between your scenes: jump straight from one scene into the next, letting time pass and locales change with no connective tissue.
Cut description that stops the story: minimize scene-setting and keep only what moves the narrative forward.
Go through your nonfiction and convert whatever you can into immediate scenes that happen before the reader's eyes.
Read your piece as a reader and cut everything that interrupts the experience: static description, summaries of what happened offstage between scenes, any glitch that breaks immersion.
Find summaries of repetitive action, like endless cups of coffee drunk while waiting, and rewrite them as one specific, concrete instance the reader can picture.
Where two scenes must be linked, bridge them with a few words of narrative summary — just enough to get the reader from one scene to the next.
Show a character’s arrogance through action, not speech: what do they do that makes the reader feel it without their saying a word?
Characterize two people at once: when one character describes another, write the description so it reveals the speaker as much as the person spoken about.
Build your story from a character rather than a plot: imagine a person so alive that what they do becomes the story itself.
Combine a physical and a psychological attribute in one portrait so each amplifies the other — brittle with arthritis, yet people stop to listen as if Moses spoke.
Probe your character across contrasting situations — strangers versus family, a famous old friend versus one down on his luck — the differences reveal who they are.
Cut the clichéd physical catalogue — facial features, breasts, hips, broad shoulders, chiseled features — it is top-of-the-head, thoughtless writing.
Cut the excess: when you characterize, stop piling on details and search for the single word or phrase that characterizes best.
Cut overused generalizations and similes — “She shuffled like a bag lady,” “She carried herself like a queen” — they pass on information but evoke nothing.
Add dramatic contrast between what your character is doing and what they are saying to themselves — the gap between act and inner voice is the drama.
Characterize with deliberate exaggeration — Laverne weighed two tons naked — since nobody takes the hyperbole literally, it communicates quickly and effectively.
Put exaggerations in a character’s mouth rather than the narrator’s — exaggeration spoken by a character is acceptable and characterizes the speaker too.
Instead of giving a character’s eye color or shape, show how they use their eyes — averting them, glaring, seeking eye contact.
Characterize through at least five channels — physical attributes, clothing and the manner of wearing it, psychological attributes and mannerisms, actions, and dialogue — not just one.
Replace clichéd exaggerations in dialogue with a fresh line that characterizes — instead of “I’ve been waiting forever,” try “my fingernails could grow an inch just waiting for you.”
Replace a wimpish protagonist: imagine an intruder who barges into your study and tells you to shut up, then write a letter from that rude, assertive, candid, slightly eccentric character to you.
Keep characterization visual whenever possible — write “He walked against an unseen wind” instead of an abstract summary.
Listen to your character’s dialogue as if they were in the room with you: do their figures of speech and expressions characterize them strongly?
Never stop your story to characterize: don’t tell the reader what your character is like — let the reader see your characters talking and doing things.
Give your character one item of clothing that stands out in the reader’s mind — a raincoat worn even when the sun is shining.
Introduce your characters before the catastrophe: readers need to know the people in the car before they see the car crash, or the events will not move them.
Characterize a character at rest: give them a posture or bearing that conveys personality without motion — “the bearing of a man who had been a soldier a long time ago.”
Make your protagonist assertive: they want something, want it badly, and want it now — readers have no interest in wimps.
Characterize through psychological attributes that connect to the story — how a character deals with friends as employees, talks in ten-mile sentences, or works a party.
Give a small role to a real, recognizable person — usually a high officeholder — using only a trace of them to jog the reader’s memory.
Set your character on first appearance: if a trait defines them — a gait, a habit of interrupting — introduce it the moment they appear.
Imagine your character with reason to shout: what would we hear? If they would never shout, what thought are they repressing?
Find the single word that carries a character’s judgment of another — like calling the man “accent” — and let it reveal the speaker, not the person described.
Choose physical characteristics that relate to your story: in a love story, a woman’s hair and a man’s voice; invert them to convey an antisexual trait.
If your story starts from a theme that obsesses you, keep your allegiance to character: imagine characters whose lives involve the theme, so the story survives.
Find every trait you currently state outright — tall, skinny, brave — and convey it through an action the character performs, so the reader feels it instead of being told it.
Fully characterize every participant in a love triangle: a one-note third character — all sex, no personality — fails to come alive and makes the relationship incredible.
When a character feels one-note, describe them with an unexpected comparison from another category — a woman walking like a young lion — and carry those traits through the book.
Make your villain mean-spirited — deriving satisfaction and even pleasure from hurting the hero or blocking their goal — not merely badly behaved.
Open a characterization with a visual image and close with the character’s conclusion — reversing the order lessens the effect.
Don’t default to “walk”: choose the verb whose nuance both characterizes and conveys a visual image — promenade, amble, scurry, dart, bolt — and make reflecting on word meanings a daily habit.
Have a character characterize a whole class of people: through their snapshot of one person, show what a whole group shares.
Give your antagonist a slightly disturbing physical mannerism — an involuntary blink, a sniff, nose-wrinkling — whose repetition grates on readers.
Decide how your antagonist behaves toward people they’ve never met — effusive charm, over-deference, discourtesy, open boredom, or arrogance.
Have your character complain bitterly about something and listen — bitter complaining speaks from the gut and reveals what is normally hidden from public view.
Make your character’s change surprising but consistent — never out of sync with what the reader knows of them.
Explore the full span of meaning of personality, disposition, temperament, individuality, and eccentricity for your character — the exercise itself improves characterization.
Imagine your adult character secretly dressed in children’s clothes and ask why — but take the character’s answer, not yours.
Before sleep, imagine a conversation between the character you are working on and a character you love from a classic; listen to what one says and how the other answers.
Rephrase top-of-the-head descriptions of your character’s clothing into visual images that say something particular about them.
Characterize through contrast — give a character a behavior that clashes with their appearance, like the immaculately dressed woman picking her nose.
Give a character attributes that go against their dominant behavior in the scene to come.
Ask whether your antagonist is curable — bad will work, but evil will provide a more profound experience for the reader.
Cut characterization so extreme it makes the character seem like a cartoon — such characters are hard to make credible in mainstream fiction.
Cut protagonists who are psychotic or habitual drunks — readers find it difficult to identify with such behavior.
Define your character’s disposition — their customary emotional response to the people and places of their world.
Make your character just different enough to interest the reader without seeming “special,” so readers from any walk of life can identify with their plight.
Think of the most eccentric person you know, imagine your character doing their most eccentric thing, then adjust it to a variation that stays in character.
Give your character an offbeat manner of behavior, dress, or speech that is peculiar to them and unlike most other people.
Ask whether your character is capable of any important eccentricity — if not, you may have picked a character readers won’t find interesting.
When you pit characters against each other, decide which emotions you are manipulating in the reader.
Make your character’s extraordinary quality evident almost immediately after they appear, unless the story’s thrust is the gradual unveiling of unusual habits or ambition.
Make your characters extraordinary rather than “perfectly ordinary” — readers don’t seek the company of people who seem like everyone else.
Check that your character’s oddity is individual behavior, not conformity to a widespread group mode — shared fashion isn’t eccentricity.
Rephrase your character’s quirk as others see it, not as the character sees it — they believe their idiosyncrasies are “perfectly normal.”
Describe your character’s singularity with the particulars of concrete detail — the traits by which others recognize them.
When you have trouble improving a characterization, you need to know more — view your character from a different perspective.
Characterize a minor character in a few words through a single action — not a description of their uniform or clothing.
Use a minor character to characterize a major player and to advance the plot at the same time.
Cut minor-character detail that fools the reader into expecting a larger role — sometimes all you want is for the reader to be able to see them.
Select one memorable characteristic that singles each minor character out from the rest of humanity — especially fleeting ones.
Characterize a minor character through the eyes of an important character.
Imagine your character in the nude, honestly and in detail — people in the nude become especially vulnerable, and a person seen realistically in the nude is immediately credible.
Unfetter your imagination — see your character flapping arms trying to fly, or walking in the snow without shoes; readers are interested in the out-of-the-ordinary.
When introducing a character who holds power in a scene, suggest their vulnerability before they exercise it; when introducing a character who will be hurt, show their strength at the outset.
Plan how your protagonist changes by the end of the novel — a risk taker may step into adulthood by learning that some risks are foolhardy.
Give your protagonist will — desire reinforced by ambition — so they drive readers through the story.
Characterize through self-contradiction — a character explaining himself in contradictory terms fascinates readers.
Scope your short story to one event or episode with room for a change of attitude toward something specific — not a profound character transformation.
Visualize your character as suddenly rather old — how would appearance, dress, and walk change? — and carry something of that into the present-age characterization.
Define your character’s temperament — their characteristic way of confronting a new day or a new development.
Weave your characters’ traits into the story as part of an action — keep your explanations out of it.
Rewrite how you describe a character’s tastes as a distinctive verbal habit — the words they use to name other people.
Give your villain a human side — a wife and child, charm — so the reader meets the person behind the evil.
Make your villain seem like a normal human being — no whips, no snarling — whose villainy is an ineradicable part of his nature.
Write what other people think but don’t say — don’t be a Pollyanna.
Ask yourself whether the conflict you've invented involves the best possible thing that could happen to your protagonist; if not, raise what is at stake.

If your conflict is small, enlarge it until it resonates: does it lead to profound unhappiness, injury, or death, or turn on an object exceedingly valuable to the main character or on an important life decision?
If your character needs to get somewhere right away, break the car down, change the weather drastically, or introduce any unexpected, uncontrollable event.
Give your characters a want that motivates them and drives their actions: the driving force of characters is their desire.
Relate your character's deepest desire to their fundamental difference from other characters, especially the antagonist.
Cause a character to be embarrassed: it will almost always create an interesting plot development.
For each important incident in your plot, note what you would normally expect to happen next, then have the exact opposite happen.
Even when your plot deviates from the norm, keep the protagonist's fierce desire and the conflict engendered by obstacles: complex plots never deviate from those.
Make your characters want something right away, even if it's only a glass of water.
Make your conflicting wants connected significantly and over something the reader will view as important, not just meaningful to the characters.
Check that your clash seems inevitable to the reader, that coincidence is not its cause, and that it takes place in a highly visible environment so the reader sees the action.
Think of what would most thwart your protagonist's want, then give the antagonist the power to thwart it.
If a scene isn't exciting enough, introduce a new character into it, especially one with something important at stake in what is happening in the scene.

Create obstacles beyond the villain: acts of nature, an unwanted intervention by a helper who makes things worse, someone blocking the protagonist for reasons of their own, or a previously absent person who returns out of the loop.
Prepare a list of every obstacle you plan to use in your plot, then ask: is the first obstacle strong enough to hook the reader, and do the obstacles build?
Make each obstacle greater than the last: as each obstacle is faced and overcome by the protagonist, an even greater obstacle must present itself.
If your protagonist wants little or has largely given up wanting, give them a want they actively pursue.

When you're stuck for character-derived plot ideas, study the classified personal ads: their writers want a relationship badly enough to advertise for it, and in describing the person they want to meet they are unknowingly describing themselves.
Plant your obstacles ahead of time so they don't seem like arbitrary devices of the author.
Make your character want something badly enough that readers root for them to attain it: the more urgent the want, the greater the reader's interest.
Put your protagonist's desire and antagonist's desire into sharp conflict: if the conflict isn't sharp, the tension will be lax.
Generate a character's fear from small things, not just mortal danger: experienced novelists do, and it creates enormous tension.
Shape your conflict so it results in a verbal or physical struggle that calls for strong scenes in which your characters clash in an exciting way.
Make the want and the opposition to it important, necessary, and urgent, so the result is the kind of conflict that interests readers.

If you write popular fiction, give your protagonist a less personal, more melodramatic want: defeating a national enemy's plans, blocking an assassin, rescuing someone close to them, or solving an important crime.
Give your conflict two-way urgency: the protagonist wants their important desire fulfilled as soon as possible, and the antagonist wants to wreck that chance just as soon.

If your character's want is too specialized, replace it with one close to universal: gaining or losing a love, achieving a lifetime ambition, seeing justice done, saving a life, seeking revenge, or accomplishing a task that at first seemed impossible.
Pick an unusual locale you know well enough to depict accurately, put a character most unlikely to show up there into it, and imagine what happens when other characters react.
Transfer the worst thing you imagined to the character in your story and ask whether it creates a suitable obstacle in your plot.
Think of the worst thing that could possibly happen to you right now, and don't censor: a writer disciplines himself to uncover, where a layman instinctively covers up.
End most chapters of your book so that they point toward the next chapter.
Start with the character rather than a preconceived plot: from the character, then the word, and from the character’s words, bring forth the action.
Characterize a character as capable of his bizarre conduct before he does it, or the act will seem ludicrous.
Let your characters do things readers crave—steal, kill, covet—rather than keeping them meek, innocent, forgiving, and peaceable, which makes readers yawn.
Distinguish a closed environment from a crucible: the locale alone does not make a crucible — add an overwhelming relationship that keeps the characters there.
Treat every coincidence in your story as a credibility risk: what enchants in life reads in fiction as the author’s contrivance.
Convert summaries into visual events the reader can see; for the summaries you keep, shorten them so the reader doesn’t lose attention.
Audit every action central to your story: is its motivation credible at the moment it happens? A major act, like kidnapping, must seem motivated as it takes place or the story reads as made up.

If the locale you chose for a scene does not add the stress of a crucible, change the location so it is difficult for one participant to leave, or add background that links the characters and raises the stress of their relationship.
Form a crucible for your plot: an environment, emotional or physical, that bonds your characters and holds them together as things heat up, so they cannot declare a truce and quit.
Make your characters' motivation to keep opposing each other greater than their motivation to run away — or place them where they cannot run: a prison cell, a lifeboat, an army, a family.
Ask whether your beginning provokes sufficient curiosity, and how soon after the start the reader reaches the engine of your piece—the point at which they decide not to stop reading.
Go after most adjectives and adverbs and all flab as an editor, not as the writer. Cut every cliché—say it new or say it straight—and cut similes or metaphors that show signs of strain.

Read your manuscript as if you were its editor and it was written by someone else: identify the weakest part, cut it, condense it if it can’t be cut entirely, or add something to its beginning that arouses the reader’s curiosity.
Cut clichés that are out of character and check that every line spoken fits the character’s background.
Rewrite a flat exchange so the talk turns tough, combative, or adversarial — such talk can be as exciting as physical action.
Rewrite dialect without odd spellings or phonetic pronunciations like “seester” — both cost the reader effort and annoy.
Choose each character’s words for their effect — “May I know your name?” signals polite formality, “You, what’s your name?” impolite aggression.
Cut echoes from your dialogue — replies that mirror the question back. Remove every line that merely repeats what was said.
Elaborate an ethnic character’s speech through content and small errors — omitted words, wrong verbs, missing articles, a foreign word understood in context — rather than phonetic spellings.
Rewrite an exchange so a few lines imply the speakers’ shared, unresolved past — no speeches at each other.
Write dialogue as a foreign tongue—a semblance of speech, not a record of it—in which directness diminishes and obliqueness sings.
Write historical dialogue as invention, not mimicry: pick the more formal and archaic elements of the period’s speech while keeping it intelligible to today’s reader.
Turn the conversation with an incidental remark — “It’s beginning to rain” — and let the response carry the plot in a new direction.
Test each line of dialogue by asking what the speaker is trying to accomplish with those exact words — a single word like “Now Ed” can admonish or warn.
Cut jargon in dialogue to a touch: a surfeit turns characterization into caricature.
Cut filler from dialogue: “uh” and other time-borrowing words are useless, and every word left must count toward characterization, story, or emotion.
Differentiate each character’s speech with markers — vocabulary, throwaway words, tight or loose wording, run-on sentences, sarcasm, poor grammar, omitted words — so no two characters sound alike.
Write dialogue for the effect of what is meant, not what is said — the reader supplies the meaning and feels the emotion it generates.
Rewrite first-person monologue so it reveals character instead of sounding like answers to a questionnaire of biographical facts.
Read your dialogue aloud in a flat monotone; rewrite any line whose words cannot do the job without expression.
Rewrite your dialogue so characters answer obliquely, not directly — the best dialogue leaves the question half-unanswered.
Rephrase a direct question so it opens the gate for an oblique answer: “Why are you giving me the third degree?” demands a reply, but “What’s this third degree?” invites one.

State the purpose of each dialogue exchange, then check whether it begins or heightens conflict, stimulates curiosity, creates tension, and builds to a climax or a change in the speakers’ relationship.
Treat dialogue as a semblance of speech, not a recording: invent exchanges that are leaner than real talk and build in tempo or content toward a climax.
Cut throwaway words and phrases — “actually,” “basically,” “you see,” “anyway” — unless you keep them deliberately as a character’s verbal tic.
Signal a character’s education or pretension with just a word or two of distinctive vocabulary — but only words that fit the character, or they will jar the reader.
Break a stretch of dense prose with dialogue — the white space makes the reader feel the story is moving faster.
Cut the manner verbs from your dialogue tags—mutter, whisper, blurt, bellow, scream—and let the words themselves carry their own decibels.
Choose each word for its precise meaning and its sound, arrange your words deliberately, and select them for effect — excellence in diction is the most important characteristic of fine writing.
Diminish a coincidence by arranging concrete detail around it — a store only one character needs, a character peering in to avoid the other — so the meeting lands as a true surprise.
Strive toward a distinctive voice or style — precision, freshness, insight, and resonance are the shared interests of writers who produce durable work.
Replace the material you would freely show friends and family with the picture you are reluctant to show — readers don’t want your photo album; they have their own.
Elucidate the background of a major action before it happens so the reader is not left guessing — what in the character’s past made the act possible?
Rewrite the places where you convey your own emotion — where you emote — so they instead stimulate an emotion in the reader, which is to evoke.
Imagine the snapshot the person you truly dislike carries and would never want you to see — and take the second thing that comes to mind, not the first.
Instead of describing your character’s terror, create the circumstances that make the reader feel the terror directly, the way Kafka does.
Describe a character’s clothing with one distinguishing item and let the reader imagine the rest, instead of listing the full outfit as if preparing a missing persons bulletin.

When you give your reader detail on character, clothing, settings, or actions, choose the single most effective detail and err on the side of too little rather than too much, so the reader’s imagination has room to work.
Treat the reader’s experience as an envelope: fill it with just enough detail to trigger the reader’s imagination, and never so much that nothing is left for it to do.
End a chapter at a moment of unresolved threat — a menace left unspecified, as in “something else can happen” — so the reader’s own anticipation does the terrorizing between chapters.
When a character’s outward action already carries the moment, cut the sentences telling the reader what the character is thinking or seeing, and trust the reader to imagine whatever fits the story.
Plant an eccentric act by escalating it in stages across earlier scenes — socks first, then a tie over the undershirt, then no pants at all — so each step is credible.
Don’t vent your emotions onto the reader; your duty is to evoke the reader’s emotions.
Convey how a person feels by describing an action rather than by stating the feeling.
Develop an idea through an anecdote involving people rather than presenting it abstractly.
Revise your portrait of a real person until they breathe on the page—name, title, and appearance alone do not make the reader know them.
In a longer work, use how your person has changed over time.
Where appropriate, evoke what your subject looked like earlier and later in life.
Revise the passage so it evokes emotion in the reader—people are moved more by what they feel than by what they understand.
Give the person’s eyes something to do—show how they look at a person or look away.
Ground the details of a scene you never witnessed in eyewitness testimony and paintings so readers trust the rendering.
Set what you report in a framework by connecting it to what has happened elsewhere or in the past, so the recorded events gain a second dimension and sight becomes insight.
Find something individual about the person’s gait or posture and put it on the page.
Check whether a reader could identify the person you’re writing about if they saw them in a group of ten; rewrite until they could.
Give the person a habit—tapping a finger, pointing eyeglasses, laughing too loud, waving hands in a particular way—that makes them more visible.
Add markers—dress, possessions, habits, routines—that signal a person’s background, and practice using them consciously a few times until it becomes a rewarding habit.
Rephrase a characterization so a single physical metaphor (like “an owl of a man”) carries the likeness while the rest of the sentence carries the psychology.
Rework your word choices until each one satisfies precision, clarity, and euphony—weigh alternatives instead of taking the first word that comes to mind.
Use your documented research not only to characterize a historical person but to give the reader a rich experience.
Lend resonance to a characterization by invoking other matters in which the person was involved.
Take risks in characterizing public figures; if a liberty doesn’t work, it will be apparent when you revise.
When you set a scene, convey the essence of the occasion—the reader gets facts, but it is the essence that conveys truth.
Build resonance into a scene so it carries what the moment means beyond the visible action—the difference between ordinary and extraordinary writing.
Make a person come alive by rendering their appearance with one specific detail.
Vitalize a person in a sentence or two by selecting one unusual characteristic, drawing on animals, fish, birds, insects, or plants for the image.
Replace a vague factual image like “dressed all in black” with particulars that carry feeling, not just the fact.
Conjure a mental snapshot so private you wouldn’t carry it in your wallet — something you wouldn’t want a paramedic, neighbor, closest friend, or family member to find.
Expect your first draft to be flawed and to need your editorial skills. Instead of despairing over how awful it reads, treat revision as your second chance to fix it.
Look closely at what you write and test each word and phrase for both accuracy and necessity.
Where one adjective cannot create the specific image, keep a second adjective or an adverb modifying the adjective, as in “heavily pregnant.”
Test each adjective for necessity: if removing it would mislead the reader, as removing “right” would in “His right eye kept blinking,” keep it.
Sweep out your adverb clusters and shorten your sentences; pace improves from both moves at once.
Cut adverbs whose meaning the verb already connotes—scribbling implies hurry, so “hurriedly” goes.
Keep paired adverbs when each conveys a distinct meaning you intend, as “heartily” and “happily” each carry their own connotation.
Test each adverb against two keep-rules: does it supply necessary information, or does it help the reader visualize the precise image? Cut the rest.
Cut empty structural fillers like “an” and “one” in “This idea is an interesting one”; “This idea is interesting” is stronger.
At your chapter endings, cut sentences that are excessively sentimental or too abstract, leaving the reader with a concrete emotion instead.
Replace clichés—tired, overused word pairs like “huffing and puffing”—with the single word that carries the meaning.
When you cut one of two paired adjectives, drop the comma with it—commas tend to slow the reading process.
Replace bland paired adjectives with a single adjective that piques the reader’s curiosity—curious, strange, eerie—one that makes them want to know why.
When a whole sentence adds nothing, cut the entire sentence—the deletion strengthens what is left and steps up the pace.
Cut the flab from your text: removing unnecessary words improves pace and strengthens the body of what remains.
Find and delete every “very” and “quite” that crept into your first draft.
When two images convey the same thing, cut one—duplicated images make the reader conscious of the craft instead of the effect, and the pace speeds up.
When a general clause restates a more specific one, delete the general clause—it says the same thing twice.
Don’t apply the one-plus-one rule to a conscious piling-up of words for effect—intentional piling adds force; accidental repetition diminishes it.
When two sentences say the same thing, cut the one that weakens the setup—keep the short first sentence so the specific image lands.
When you cut excess verbiage, keep words that help the reader visualize the precise image you are trying to fashion, even when their meaning is implied.
Find two sentences where the second merely names what the first already implies, and merge them into one faster sentence.
Cut your narrator’s generalization about what he has just shown—the specific scene is enough, and the generalization distracts.
Cut adjectives that state the obvious or add nothing to the image—“quaint and white” weakens “an old man in sculptured soap.”
Apply the formula “one plus one equals a half”: saying the same thing over and over minimizes its impact, so cut the redundancy.
Become your own editor: publishers do far less line editing than they used to, so catching redundancy is the writer’s job.
Cut redundancies where one term includes the other—“my parents, Mom and Dad”—and keep one or the other, not both.
Never choose between adjectives arbitrarily. Use words for their precise meaning in context; that is the mark of a good writer.
Cut words that restate what another word already encompasses, like “private and public” before “life,” and drop phrases that add unnecessary information.
Strip every adjective and adverb from your manuscript, then readmit only the few that survive careful testing.
Be as tough on yourself in eliminating unnecessary words as an editor would be—the best writers are the toughest on themselves.
Find every place where you used two adjectives with a single noun and eliminate one of them, keeping the more concrete or more visual adjective.
When two adverbs modify one verb, try eliminating both—the unadorned verb is direct and picks up the pace.
Compile your own list of flab words—“however,” “almost,” “perhaps,” “there is”—and sweep your text for each one.
Write your story so it seems to be happening now, no matter when it is set.
Read your flashback and judge whether it interrupts the reader's experience of the present story. The reader wants the ride, not a look at the machinery.
Rewrite your flashback as a scene with characters in conflict, however short it is.
Cut the flashback if it doesn't markedly enhance the present story. If it isn't important to the story, you may not really need it.
Rewrite the flashback as an immediate scene the reader witnesses, depicted exactly as the present story would be — not an offstage narrative summary.
Slip into your flashback quickly and unobtrusively so the reader never sees it coming and doesn't skip pages.
Make the first sentence of your flashback arresting.
Purge every "had" and "then" from your flashback and write it in the straight past tense of your present scenes — "I remembered", not "I had been remembering".
Open your flashback with dialogue early, even if the flashback is short — dialogue is always an immediate scene.
Introduce your flashback by seguing from the present scene into the past as inconspicuously as possible, rather than announcing the shift directly.
Conclude your flashback with a line space, a time marker like "One week later ...", or dialogue that restarts the present scene.
Let your character's thoughts, including thoughts of the past, interrupt the present scene to enrich the character and give the scene texture.
Build any past material that exceeds quick thoughts in an ongoing scene into a flashback scene that stands on its own — not a narrative of what happened elsewhere.
Fashion a flashback to increase suspense: insert it into a long confrontation scene so it postpones the outcome.
Rewrite the background information as present dialogue so the reader witnesses a dramatic scene now and you eliminate the need for a flashback.
Convey the background the reader needs through a character's silent thoughts during a present scene instead of a flashback.
Give the reader knowledge of your character before the crisis arrives — you have to know the people in the car before you see the crash.
Do a focused reading of your manuscript as a hunter on assignment, hunting for specific errors and omissions rather than reading as a reader.
Track the objects in your scene: when a character orders coffee, the coffee must appear — rewrite scenes where a prop vanishes between request and delivery.
Borrow the candor of another: quote someone else’s daring words — pass the candor chalice — to make the candid point yourself.
Know that as a nonfiction writer you are more exposed than the novelist, who hides a little under the presumption that he is making things up — dare anyway.
Distinguish forthrightness from sensationalism: what your writing requires is honesty of a kind that gets self-suppressed by the public, not tabloid shock.
Find the one concrete incident in your material that can serve as the fulcrum of your piece and build the essay around it.
Take the oath to write nothing inoffensive: the success of an article or nonfiction book rests on your courage in revealing normally unspoken things about yourself or your society.
Elaborate the hidden reality of your own work: write about what actually happens in your field — its normally private, unspoken acts — with precision, clarity, grace, and candor.
Put what you actually think into the text: overcome your natural reluctance to say the things you think — fig leaves have no place on the minds of the best writers.
Rewrite toward the unspeakable: what makes writing at its best interesting is your willingness to say things that people don’t ordinarily say.
Give your hero faults and your villain charm: the hero’s faults bring him to life, and the villain’s charm is the honey with which he lures the innocent.
When a word’s meaning is fuzzy to you, stop and ask what it precisely means — “human” is not “humane” — and replace words chosen off the top of your head out of speed.
Use immediate scenes wherever you can in your nonfiction, and put your first immediate scene on page one.
Infect your reader with anxiety, stress, and tension, for the conditions they deplore in life they relish in fiction.
Replace every approximate word with the precisely right word: delight in le mot juste and never let the near-miss word pass in your own work.
When you want to convey an emotion, search for words that evoke it — “lilting house” rather than the direct, obvious “happy house.”
Write characters understood in depth, engaged in activities resonant with the ambiguities and stresses of life, so that they persist in the reader’s mind after the reading is over.
When your scene is literary rather than commercial fiction, make the characters' differing scripts more subtle instead of broadly clashing.
When you devise a locale for a scene, choose a closed environment — it will invariably increase the tension — and think of that locale when you are first imagining your characters.
Give the animal in your story a distinctive particularity, as you would a human character, and tie that characteristic to the story.
Give the animal in your story a clear want of its own instead of making it a passive recipient of the human characters' wants.
Cut the mechanical description of sexual activity from your love scene; it will not arouse readers and fails to evoke a loving experience between people.
Before writing your love scene, consider what the reader is feeling at each moment; the primary erogenous zone is in the reader's head.

Consider your love scene from the point of view of each partner even when writing from one character's disciplined point of view, so the reader understands the relationship better than either lover does.
Build your love scene from tension and tenderness: postpone the consummation as long as credibility permits and keep the likely outcome hidden from the reader.
Rewrite your love scene so the attraction between the lovers seems new, even in a longstanding relationship; no love scene should repeat a familiar ritual.
Delay the consummation of your love scene and build anticipation through minutiae—small actions and details—while the possibility of contact hangs in the air.
Cut the sentimentality from your love scene—any emotion that is exaggerated or affected and obviously designed to win the reader's sympathy—and aim instead for a depth of feeling.
Consider putting both the gain and the loss of love in the same story; together they are doubly powerful.
Make each of your lovers vulnerable in a different way, and evoke the reader's feelings through what they say and do rather than telling the reader what they feel.
Derive your love plot and what happens in your love scene from your characters' motivations; remind yourself that plot grows out of character.
Give each of your lovers one thing that distinguishes their physical appearance, and a distinctive way of dressing.
Search your love story for root conflicts based on character and upbringing, and add a surface crisis that increases the tension if your lovers are not already at a moment of crisis.
Ask whether your love story has enough friction between the lovers to hold the reader's interest, but not so much that the reader stops believing they are in love.
Write ten brief exchanges of dialogue between two lovers that make the reader feel both that they are quarreling and that they are lovers, not ex-lovers.
Write your best scenes with more than one thing going on at a time, as in a quarrel that is unmistakably a lovers' exchange.
For your older lovers, keep a hovering notion that they do not have all the time in the world, include the need for companionship, and add a touch that enhances the poignancy.
Imagine your love scene from the perspective of each partner; if you are a man, give special thought to the woman's perspective, and if a woman, to the man's.
Enrich your love scene by having one of the participants gain an insight about the other person.
Plant a meaningful object before your love scene, keep it unnoticed until an important juncture, and let one lover's reaction to it turn the scene so the other must rekindle the relationship.
Introduce an unexpected misunderstanding that deepens the more one lover tries to clear it up, then bring in a third character who either worsens or resolves the impasse.
Interrupt your love scene with a significant thought or memory; it can be more effective than a loud external event.
Write a poignant love scene in which the lovers never come close enough to touch; a love scene and a sex scene are not the same.
Cut the multiple sexual acts from your erotic scene; a single act kept at bay and stretched out can have a marked erotic effect.
Before writing your erotic scene, be clear about the relationship between the couple and what the sexual intimacy accomplishes in your story.
Give every sexual encounter in your story a meaning for at least one of the characters, or it does not belong in the story.
In your one-night stand scene, ask why each participant is doing this and how each reacts during and after, so the encounter conveys something about each character.
Write the sexual encounter that begins a love affair as a back-and-forth experience, not a straight line; let digressions that serve the scene heighten and extend it.
Have your character put himself down in a way that raises him in the reader's eyes; self-deprecation can signal insight and make him a more interesting lover.
Write the tension of arousal in short sentence snippets, then render the breakthrough as one long breathless extended sentence.
For lovers who have made love before, add a surprise, the opposite of the expected, or an intrusion that stops the inevitable outcome.
Break up any scene of continuous lovemaking with thoughts, actions, digressions, and delays pertinent to the story; list each character's concerns and make them different to maximize tension.
Give each of your characters a different script for their love scene, as in the Actors Studio technique.
As you revise your love scene, test each part of it for what you believe the reader is feeling at that moment.
Rephrase the explicit moments in your love scene so the reader's imagination does the work.
Replace violent or graphic moments in your love scenes with small actions or a few well-chosen words; they move the reader more.
In a love between mismatched or unlikely partners, generate the reader's emotion from the conflict of repugnance slowly overcome by affection.
Rewrite characterization so a character’s action — sending food back, overtipping, watching everyone — reveals background in a single stroke.
Use a character’s attitude — like expecting to be insulted or mugged by every passerby — as a marker of background.
Examine your two most important characters for social or class differences; if you have neglected such differences, add some that arouse emotion.

Ask yourself what inherited trait most shaped your protagonist, what family custom haunts him, which habit he has failed to break, and what in the villain’s upbringing made him what he is — the answers supply useful markers.
Give your main character inherited or trained baggage — upbringing, customs, temperament — and show whether they can overcome it.
Delete cliché markers — the American tourist abroad hunting for hamburgers — and replace them with details that still carry surprise.
Use clothing to signal whether two characters belong to the same world — mismatched dress tells the reader they are not together.
Describe a character’s clothing as a reaction to the surroundings of the scene — dress that clashes with the setting signals phoniness or contempt.
Give each character markers — easily identified signals of cultural and social background — so the reader identifies their different worlds quickly.
Characterize instantly through public conduct — how a character behaves with children in public is an immediate marker.
Recheck your markers against today’s readers — class signifiers that once worked have diffused in time, so choose details whose connotations still register.
Run each small detail you give a character — gum chewing, an ankle bracelet, a man’s rings — past the question of what it suggests about their background.
Build the conflict of your scenes and whole plots on the cultural differences between your characters — differences are more important than similarities.
Squelch your emotional reactions to your material consciously so you gain enough distance to use it in your work as a writer.
Use what a character drinks and eats, and where, as a background marker — beer and rye versus Scotch and Perrier signal different worlds.
Cut any marker that needs a paragraph of explanation — a marker should convey its point instantly or it is not working.
Put two characters of sharply different backgrounds in the same story — readers’ emotions commit quickly — then step back and let the drama of their differences explode without mediating.
Cut the sentence that explains what a marker means — show only the detail, the fingernails, and let the reader draw the inference.
Characterize through how your character speaks — vocabulary, accent, verbal tics, clichés — as markers of background.
Rephrase sentences that state a character’s background so the content of the character’s speech — what they know and care about — shows it instead.
Discern your characters’ differences with subtlety instead of sorting them into good guys and bad guys.
Show, in the interaction of your characters, the gap between what they profess and how they act; deal with the unspoken rather than the acceptable.
Articulate what makes your most memorable passage so good, and use that insight as a clue for what to do with your weakest part.
Write a metaphor by bringing together two words or phrases that do not ordinarily belong together so that their proximity conveys a fresh meaning.
Don’t be afraid of a long stretch in a metaphor: if it makes its point instantly, the distance between the two things is what gives it power.
Search your draft for mixed metaphors—two or more unrelated metaphors unsuccessfully combined—and rewrite one side of the image so the comparison holds together.
Use a metaphor to set the mood of a scene: describe the setting through an image that carries the feeling you want the reader to share.
In a nonfiction piece, find a concrete image that could carry a metaphor and add one to enhance the prose.
Audit the density of figures of speech in your draft: if they are overdone, they backfire—cut until each comparison earns its place.
After cutting or changing the weakest part, find the new weakest part that has taken its place; improve it, or cut it and stitch together what comes immediately before and after.

Examine the cast of your piece for two people, parties, organizations, or entities in conflict; where the conflict is not immediately apparent, bring the conflicting elements closer together and highlight it, actual or potential.

Check your article, story, or book for dramatic conflict: the reader's interest flags wherever you failed to keep in mind that dramatic conflict has been the basis of stories from the beginning of time.
Build and maintain suspense in your nonfiction through a consistent point of view in which the reader learns only what the narrator knows, and learns it when the narrator learns it.
At the planning stage, consider placing your two adversaries in a crucible — a situation that holds them together more than anything drives them apart — so their conflict cannot end in a truce.
Cut facts that unnecessarily diminish suspense early in your piece.

Structure your nonfiction piece around somebody wanting something, facing obstacles, trying to get it, and finally getting or not getting it — make the conscious use of desire the engine of the telling.

When preparing to write any passage or scene involving two people, focus on their differing intentions (or scripts) so their conflict positions itself in adversarial situations where conflict is inherent.
Rewrite your first paragraph so it arouses curiosity by withholding one piece of information until a bit later.
Humanize the people in your story by name and a couple of humanizing particulars before anything happens to them, particularizing as often as possible.
Hold back from giving the conclusion first: starting with the outcome telegraphs the story and spoils it, even though giving the conclusion first is our instinct in life.
Plant the desire before the thwart: conflict can arise from a thwarted desire, but the reader must already know what was wanted for the thwarting to move them.
Convert any sentence in your piece to a question that will arouse curiosity rather than satisfy it.

Raise the importance of what your subject wants: the more important the objective, the bigger the conflict will seem when obstacles block the want — even an unattainable want can stimulate the reader's emotions.
Handle the story so that at the end the reader draws his own conclusion — provide the conflict for interest but let the reader make the judgment.
Repeat a key name or phrase deliberately — the purposeful repetition of “Mount St. Vincent” — to help set up suspense.
Separate the two parts of an action into distinct sentences — the order given, then the refusal — because the separation itself creates the tension.
Write short sentences and short paragraphs in your tense passages to increase tension, and resist the temptation to rush to a conclusion.
Stretch a tense situation, often a confrontation between persons or groups, out over paragraphs and pages — the continuation of tension is what keeps it alive.
Create suspense by making the reader expect something to happen and then holding off: suspense occurs when what the reader expects is not happening yet because you are holding off.
Heighten suspense by switching to a different part of the story — another person, another thread — before the reader learns what they want to know.

Keep the difference between tension and suspense in mind as you build your piece: suspense arouses anxious uncertainty about what might happen, while tension involves the sudden onset of stress, strain, or pressure.
Create tension by the simple mention of a time or date that carries dread — “It was four o’clock in the morning” works because it is an hour when most people are asleep.
Describe an action that arouses curiosity but do not explain it in the same paragraph.
Set up a question or controversy in your story and do not answer or resolve it immediately.
Before you begin writing, determine whether any of the people in your story want something badly, and move that material up to the beginning to touch a match to the reader's emotions.
If your climax rescues the protagonist by coincidence or a deus ex machina, cut the device and find a credible way out — those devices fool no one.
Consciously try to create stress for the reader—some delicious tension—by adapting fiction’s tension techniques to your nonfiction.

Gain objectivity about your own work by replacing your name on a fresh title page with an admired author’s name and reading your manuscript through that author’s eyes; if that fails, use an author you dislike and go at the manuscript with a vengeance to root out unmotivated acts and coincidence.
Open by personifying your subject in an incident involving an individual rather than in abstract statement.
Find the emotional root of your book in your secret snapshot and put that image on the page — start the story there, so it becomes a moving experience rather than a plot told from the outside.
Separate your originality into its two components—the originality of what you say and the originality of the way you say it—and clarify which one is distinctive in your current work.
Go through a passage and examine each word for its necessity, precision, and clarity; cut or replace any word that fails one of the three.
Imagine yourself on a rooftop with the townspeople below, allowed to shout down one last sentence—the sentence the world will remember you by—and write that sentence down.
Test your sentence: could any person you know have said it? Revise it until you are convinced no one else could have said that sentence.
Try making your sentence outrageous, then try turning it into a question, and compare which version is stronger.
Imagine the person you love most strongly disagreeing with your sentence; add a second sentence answering their disagreement, and make sure it is stronger than the first.
Imagine your greatest enemy challenging your sentence; revise it so that your statement is incontrovertible and your enemy cannot take the last word.
Revise your sentence so that it could be whispered and still heard, and notice whether the whisper version turns out stronger than the shouted one.
Lay out all the versions of your sentence; combine the virtues of one into another, then choose the version that is most original—the one least likely to have been written by someone else.
Distrust the sentence that comes first: hone, change, and polish the words of a single sentence to test all of its possibilities.
If you start from someone else’s secret snapshot, choose one you would never be allowed to see under any circumstance.
Pick up the pace of a scene with a quick exchange of adversarial dialogue, letting the lines get clipped and each paragraph hold a single short sentence.
When revising, find scenes that don’t work as well as you had hoped and consider skipping them entirely — if removing the scene propels the pace, you turn a liability into an asset.
Jump-cut from one scene to the next without the in-between matter of travel and transition — close the door, line space, next scene — because showing the getting-there is a drag and boring.
Build purposeful slowdowns into your book from time to time, because readers, like athletes, must catch their breath.
Follow each cliffhanging chapter ending with a chapter that moves to a different location or has different characters — it sustains suspense and also increases the pace of your story.
Step up your pace by shortening sentences and paragraphing more frequently; the two together accelerate the pace even more than either alone.
Flip forward past a scene the reader anticipates — end the chapter before it happens and open the next elsewhere — so the scene lives only in the reader’s imagination and the pace quickens.
Skip the routine steps of an action and jump from one significant beat to the next — “skipping for effect” — even if that eliminates two thirds of the words.
Rewrite for particularity: to be specific is not as precise as to be particular — replace the merely concrete with the particular.
Give a character a methodical, particularized action — like moving his gaze deliberately from eyes to hair to chin to ears — that disconcerts others and reveals his nature.
Characterize an individual through particularity — how they look, dress, or speak — without resorting to clichés or generalizations.

Audit a passage of your writing for detail that individualizes: find the particulars that differentiate one person from another, one act from another, one place from any others like it. Where the detail is generic, particularize it.
Let dialogue particularize a character: give a character a line that reveals a trait — like Joe’s "Is it in the same town?" revealing his sense of humor.
Go word by word through a passage and demand precision of meaning — le mot juste, exactly the right word.
Convey a trait like "Vernon was a heavy smoker" through particularized evidence — how he coughs, how others treat him — rather than stating the generalization.
If you deal with a character's hands, give them something particular to do — like a hand that periodically checks for itself — instead of leaving them at a loss.
Find the two most particular words in your sentence — like "bald pink knees" — and make sure the sentence would turn ordinary without them.

Turn an ordinary appearance sentence into one that characterizes through a measurable, comparative particular — "Cecilia’s skirts were three inches shorter than her age allowed" instead of "Cecilia wore short skirts."
Particularize through your viewpoint character's perception: instead of saying a smile is like an implant, have the character think it is an implant.
Sweep the abstractions out of your prose, for readers are attracted by particularity.
If an ordinary object matters to your story, particularize it — its location, size, color, how it moves — so the reader's attention is called to it.

Revise an opening that lacks particularity: use actions where possible, have people talk or think in particulars, make locale, objects, and people distinctive and visible, use other senses, and make it ominous if you can.
Work on one paragraph at a time; perfect a single paragraph of particularity and use it as the model for the whole book.

Replace a general statement about a place ("The apartment was bigger than they ever expected") by stretching out particulars — the echo of a voice, the height of the ceiling, carved plaster angels — so the reader experiences the place along with the characters.
Practice particularizing in your letters and personal correspondence, replacing generalizations and clichés, so the habit carries over into your work.
Audit every detail you have added: none should be waste words; each must have a purpose, such as making a transaction credible. Cut the particulars that merely decorate.
When a character repeats an action like laughing within a few pages, particularize each instance instead of repeating "She laughed" — make each laugh distinct.
When a cliché offers itself, sharpen it with an unexpected, precise phrase — "the exquisitely perfect last second" instead of "the last second."

Resist the pressure to clip language short when your aim is to provide an experience for the reader: "The apartment was large" doesn't do it. Keep the extra words that make the experience of the action possible and credible.
Choose adjectives and adverbs for the particular sound of words — branches that swoosh and thump, gravel that pops — rather than cutting them all on principle.
When a person comes into view, don't describe him all at once: delay part of the description, start at a distance, then notice more. Use the same staged particularization for places.
Catch yourself writing top-of-the-head — the cliché or the generalization that comes first — and replace it with a sentence that particularizes in an interesting way.
Improve your work beyond the requirements of your editor or the public — hunt precise nuances and listen to the sound of words instead of stopping at good enough.
Plant a character’s motivation ahead of time before she acts for your convenience — if the plot needs her at the mall, her reason for going must be planted in advance.
Decide which of your actions would seem unconvincing without ground, and plant only those: a punch thrown in retaliation needs no planting, the tripping that provoked it does.
Before a character performs a feat of strength, plant the physical capability earlier — establish that he is a six-foot-three weightlifter before he picks a man up and throws him over a railing.
Plant a character’s motive in a single line of dialogue with a touch of humor, as in: “I’m not going to go on a shopping spree ever again. After today.”
Check your point of view discipline: have you avoided telling how a character feels and relied on actions to make the reader experience the emotion?
In first person, rewrite any line that sounds like you the author rather than the character speaking.
Write first-person narration as the character making a case for himself — his view of himself, the others, the world — not as neutral reporting.
Use first person when your protagonist does horrible things — it can draw the reader's emotions, even empathy, into the character despite his acts.
Test your scene's point of view by converting it: third person is first person with "he" or "she" substituted for "I" — see whose eyes the scene is really seen through.
Limit how many characters' POVs the reader enters in a short span — too many shifts in quick succession make the experience dizzying.
Develop the "I" character until he is sufficiently different from you.
Check every image against your POV character's physical position — cut or rewrite any description from a vantage the character cannot have.
When each chapter uses a different character's POV, choose for each scene the character most affected by that scene's events.
When your first-person narrator reads another character's feelings, mark the report as his interpretation — what he believes, not the other character's view.
Make your narrator the protagonist or a principal character directly involved in the action — he can even be the villain of the piece.
Reveal a first-person narrator's looks without the mirror cliché: let him think about his looks or changes in them, or have another character remark on them in dialogue.
Do not mix points of view within the same scene, chapter, or novel — sticking to one point of view intensifies the reader's experience.
Cut the preface: readers skip it and miss essential information — develop that material skillfully inside the story itself.
If your first-person narrator takes the reader into his confidence, don't let him withhold an essential secret — the reader will feel cheated.
Before writing objectively, know that complete objectivity is sterile of emotion — reserve it for stories that are mainly action.
When your first-person narrator reports an offstage scene he didn't witness, motivate the reporting and keep the report visual.
In omniscient POV, rewrite any passage where the reader hears the author talking instead of experiencing the story — the mode lacks discipline, so guard your credibility.
Choose the omniscient POV only if your authorial voice has personality, authority, some wisdom, and ideally a fresh sense of humor — the author must be quite a character to manage it.
Choose first person when your protagonist is highly intelligent or perceptive, so his complex thoughts reach the reader directly and intimately.
Establish the limitation of your third-person POV and stick to it — the restraint becomes an advantage, a discipline.
In first person, reveal the narrator's good qualities through his actions and other characters' speech, not through self-description.
If your draft isn't satisfying you, set it aside and rewrite it from another point of view — third to first, omniscient to third or first.
Cut scenes your first-person character wasn't a witness to — he can't know what goes on beyond his ken.
Shelve the second-person point of view: involve the reader emotionally through identification with a character, not by addressing him as "you."
If you shift point of view between parts or chapters, establish and clearly identify the new point of view at the outset of each part or chapter.
Scan your story for any slip in point of view and correct it — one slip can hurt a story badly, and several can be fatal.
When your first-person character is reluctant to reveal a secret, have another character strip the secret from him in heated conversation.
Before choosing first person for a story about surviving life-threatening dangers, weigh the lost suspense: the narrator must survive to finish the story.
Focus on the POV of one character at a time and sustain it; if readers must know what everybody thinks, use the looser omniscient form instead.
Write third person consistently from one character's point of view at a time, though you may report what any character hears, smells, touches, or tastes.
Don't put thoughts into a character's head that are beyond that character's intelligence or capabilities.
Decide whose story this is and focus on individuals — the reader wants to know whose story he is following, and a story about everybody is a story about nobody.
Break up any quoted speech that runs more than three sentences — insert something visual, however slight, between the chunks.
Edit quoted material toward the color of the speaker’s words — expletives and grammatical howlers included — neither a verbatim transcript nor a straightened-out version.
If you find yourself inventing dialogue in nonfiction, redirect that instinct into a play, novel, or movie, where invented speech belongs.
Break a long quote with a seemingly inconsequential physical detail: a cough humanizes the speaker, a pointed glance implies conflict.
Cut reported speech freely: you are not obligated to reproduce every word, only to preserve the speaker’s meaning.
Never intentionally misquote and never invent dialogue: fabricated attributed speech is a highly visible sign of untrustworthy writing.
Keep quoted speech rough: few people speak in complete grammatical sentences, and perfectly formed sentences come across to the reader as made up.

Cut excess quotation from an interview: keep only what reveals the character of the speaker or defines subject matter, preserve what is confrontational, colorful, or especially appropriate, and ditch the rest.
Treat dialogue as a danger in nonfiction: use only direct quotes that sound real and can be substantiated.
After fixing the larger problems and hunting down the smaller ones, take time away from the manuscript, then read it as a reader rather than an editor.

Audit what you read for pleasure — the field and the quality of language you require of books is what you will write. Do not expect your work to succeed in a field you don’t habitually read for pleasure.
Bring the snapshot image back at each danger your protagonist faces, so the reader carries it through the whole story.
Remove the padding—unnecessary digressions and overly extensive patches of description—from your manuscript, since you always strengthen text when you remove the padding.
