Instead of narrating an unmotivated action — he went for a walk — rephrase it as a line of dialogue that gives the character a reason, like: “These new shoes are not going to get broken in if I sit around the house.”
Give your work resonance by weaving in reverberations of other times, places, important events, or influential people.
Put aphorisms in a character’s dialogue only if you are sure the character is the kind who could and would spout aphorisms on occasion.
If an aphorism is in the author’s voice, put it in the third-person or omniscient point of view, never the first-person point of view of a character.
Choose names for your characters and phrases that carry built-in associations — biblical or otherwise — so they reverberate before the story explains them.
Open with a bold philosophical statement so its resonance carries into the sentences and paragraphs that follow.

In nonfiction, name your chapters with phrases that resonate — an allusion that evokes a familiar opposite, or a metaphor — so the effect lands twice: in the table of contents and at the heads of chapters.
Give a character the authentic, specialized thoughts of their profession so the resonance of those thoughts confirms the character’s reality.
Cut excessive preliminaries — author’s notes, prefaces, multiple epigraphs — an excess can read as defensive.
Lend importance to an ordinary day or moment by pairing it with a metaphor that draws on death or some vast, final scale.
Choose an epigraph that conveys the larger import of your work, so the work itself needn’t become didactic.
Aim for resonance that comes from the writing itself — the visual sweep of the language — not only from borrowed devices like names, epigraphs, or titles.
Keep public and historical figures in your story fleeting — appearing only briefly — and cut any attempt to reproduce them at length, especially their dialogue.
Exaggerate a perception — hyperbole — to lend resonance to what might otherwise seem ordinary.
Open your story by invoking your protagonist’s death — or the feeling of it approaching — to give the work resonance from the outset.
Borrow the language of liturgy or religious ritual to lend resonance to a key scene.
Plant omens early in your narrative to seed suspense.
Title the parts of your book so the names resonate even before the reader encounters the first sentence.
When you describe a birthplace or formative setting, make the description go a long way toward explaining the person’s life and work rather than merely detailing the place.
Invent plausible professional-sounding theory — technobabble — to authenticate a character and their profession.
Write what other people sometimes think but don’t say — or don’t allow themselves to think.
Let the characters play out the scene in front of you as you write — decide their scripts, not their lines, in advance.
Match the device to the scope: plan individual scenes by giving characters clashing scripts, but plot the whole work around a crucible that binds the characters together.
Take a scene from any novel you are reading and jot down the script — the intent — of each character in it.
Define each character's 'script' as their intent in the scene — not the actual lines of dialogue — and keep that instruction brief.

Before you write a scene, make a note of each character's script and make sure the scripts are different and at odds; if a third character enters, give that character a script different from the other two.
Give the characters in each scene you write different scripts — different intentions for that scene — so their goals clash and the scene turns dramatic.

Elaborate a character’s feeling into a sequence of small actions and a stray thought, the way a writer setting a yellow pad and a pen on the desk before an important call shows nerves without ever naming them.
Rewrite your backstory: show what happened before the story began rather than telling it in narrative summary or in a flashback, and bring offstage events onstage.
Show a condition or a change of mood through color alone, the way “the color of cold is blue” shifting to black deep beneath the Arctic water makes the change ominous.

Cut any passage that interrupts the reader’s experience to convey a character’s background or anything else the author seems to be supplying — that interruption is telling, not showing, and it starts the reader skipping.

Rewrite a flat action so that it gives the reader a sense of what the character desperately wants, the way walking “as if against an unseen wind, hoping someone would stop him” shows far more than “He took a walk.”
Check every passage against the test: does it give the reader an experience, or does it merely pass on information from the author? What readers want from writing is to experience it.
Treat what a character feels as the one danger area for telling: check that feelings are shown, never reported, before you worry about any other hazard.

Find any line where one character tells another what the second character already knows and rewrite it — unless it is an accusation, one character should never tell another what the second character already knows.
When information in your work sounds like the author’s intervention, come up with a simile or a metaphor that shows what you are trying to tell.
Change your mind-set: stop telling what happened somewhere else and start creating an experience for the reader by showing what happened.
Replace an emotion name like “He was nervous” with the action that shows it, such as “He tapped his fingers on the tabletop.”

Replace a general statement like “She boiled water” with particular, visual actions — putting the kettle on the stove, filling it from the faucet, humming until the whistle cuts her short — since the key to the improvement is particularity.
When you shape your showing image, prefer the compression of a metaphor — “the kelp of her own hair” — over the comparison of a simile — “her hair was like kelp.”
Scan your manuscript for passages where you are consciously or not reporting a story instead of showing it — reporting rather than showing is one of the chief reasons novels are rejected.

Ask yourself of the passage: Are you allowing the reader to see what’s going on? Is the author talking at any point? Can you silence the author with an action that shows what a character feels? Are you naming emotions instead of conveying them by actions?
Show what your character sees, hears, smells, touches, and tastes through actions rather than describing them, and convey feelings through actions above all.

Rephrase the information you need to plant so it arrives subtly through a natural-sounding remark between characters, the way “Do you think Henry would look more like a doctor if he grew a beard?” quietly reveals that Henry is a doctor.
Audit your passage for the three areas where telling most intrudes: what happened before the story began, what a character looks like, and what a character sees, hears, smells, touches, and tastes.

Rewrite every sentence that states a character’s trait, like “Helen was a wonderful woman, always concerned about her children,” as a visible action, the way Helen parking the car and taking a child by each hand shows her concern without being told.
Transform information passed on in a nonfiction vein into a visual scene, choosing visual details — a blush on a freckled face, a too-small crown, two hairpins — so the author is no longer telling.
Test whether a passage is showing rather than telling by determining if it is visual — can the reader see it happening?
Reread your draft for spots of bare-bones writing that could be improved by a simile or metaphor you hadn’t thought of when drafting, and add one.
Find similes and metaphors in your draft that are clichés tired from overuse, and rephrase them into fresh comparisons.
Read each simile and metaphor in your draft and ask whether it deflects your reader’s attention from the story to the words on the page; if it does, cut or replace it.
Find a flat, adverb-driven statement in your draft and rewrite it as a simile that connects two things previously unconnected, so the comparison keeps its savor.
Scan your manuscript for similes and metaphors that show strain or are inaccurate, and cut them.
Find a scene that relies only on sight and sound and rewrite it so your characters also touch, taste, and smell — a character stripped of these has lost part of their humanity.
Listen to the sounds in your scene and write them as you actually hear them, not as the clichés like "meow" or "thwack" — find the sound your reader will recognize but has never seen in print.
Mark where sound stops in your scene and write the pauses, the momentary silences — the absence of sound that makes music possible.
Render smells accurately: particularize what each place or object smells like — rubber bands have a marked odor, an old book smells musty — instead of leaving the sense vague.
Use smell to help your reader experience a setting: what odor would draw them into the room — fresh-baked bread drifting like an invitation?
Give a character a habitual scent that does the characterizing for you — a signature perfume that tells the reader they use too much of it.
Look for the smell that is absent from your scene — like the rose bred of its smell — and use that absence to carry meaning.

Blindfold yourself, empty your pocket or purse onto a table, and describe each object by touch alone, as if to someone from another planet — you can't say it feels like plastic, you have to particularize.
Go through every scene you write and use the sense of touch at least once.
From memory, describe the foods of your last meal to a guest who has never tasted them — invent similes and metaphors so their taste buds pop, and never feed cardboard meals to your characters.

Write a moment where a character senses something beyond the five senses — a door closing when there is no wind, someone in the room who is not there — in mainline as well as mystery and suspense fiction.
Your first visual impression of a person or place is usually a cliché — look again for the distinguishing detail, the particularity, the thing nobody has seen quite that way before.
Switch the sense to make a metaphor: describe what is seen through another sense, as when a character can "smell the difference" — the switch lands the point quickly.
Check your sensory characterizations: each one must be an action, somebody doing something — never stop the story to characterize or to use the senses.

Test your snapshot: would you carry it in your wallet or purse? If yes, it is not secret enough — the snapshots that work best are embarrassing, revelatory, or involve a strong and continuing stimulus to memory.
Value-test your snapshot: would its owner pay to keep you from seeing it, and would you pay to see it? If you would pay to see it, readers may pay for your book.
Check whether any friend or neighbor could have a snapshot just like yours; if so, change it to one that only you have, so your writing could not come out of anyone else’s closet.
Listen to the sound of your words as you write literary fiction — sound can contribute to the effect even when readers rarely notice it working.
Give an object a human characteristic with a single word, as “the street-lamp’s vigil” gives the lamp vigilance — compress a metaphor to one word.
When a character's life crisis demands immediate action, make certain the action backfires and prolong the crisis.
Audit every chapter ending except the last: does it arouse the reader's interest anew and thrust them forward into the next chapter?
Review your chapter lengths: keep chapters short so the story seems to move faster, but avoid any chapter under three printed pages.
Scan your novel for narrative summaries of offstage happenings between scenes and cut them: the reader's interest is in the scenes, not the interstices between them.
Look at your list of scenes, find the weakest one where your own interest flags, and cut it; then repeat with the next weakest. You are not a scene preserver.
Set up something that cries for resolution, then deliberately dance away from the reader's problem, dealing with other things and prolonging the reader's desperate need for resolution.

Check your scene against these sources of anxious uncertainty: a prospective or immediate danger to a character, an unwanted confrontation, an old fear about to become real, or a life crisis demanding immediate action.
Find an action the reader urgently wants to happen, then delay it by having the character think about the past before acting.
When your character overcomes an immediate danger, don't eliminate the danger—make them face an even greater one instead.
Recast the outcome of each major turn so it does not take the reader where he wants to go.
Put your protagonist in serious trouble, then refuse to rescue them: hang your hero by his fingertips and leave him hanging as long as the story can bear.
If your character is apprehensive about an unwanted confrontation, hold it off as long as possible.
Open your story and find the moment that arouses the reader's curiosity about what will happen next; then hold that curiosity alive, unresolved, for as long as you can.
Count the lines of suspense running through your book: are two or three characters in unresolved trouble at once, each in a different location?
Reorganize your chapters in any order that accelerates the suspense of the whole, keeping time moving only forward and avoiding shifts that disturb the reader.
Chart each scene on its own line: its location (different from the preceding scene, if possible), its principal character, and the action in brief; if a scene has no action, it isn't really a scene.
End a scene with your character in serious trouble, then start the next scene in a different location with a different character, leaving the reader in suspense about the first.
Pick up a suspense or thriller you couldn't put down and study its chapter endings: note how each ends on a suspenseful note and throws the reader forward into the next chapter.
In literary fiction, keep the suspense subtle but still ensure each chapter ending arouses the reader's curiosity about what happens next.
End each chapter with your hero or heroine in unresolved trouble, as serials and soap operas do, so the reader wants to see what happens next.
Find the moment your reader wants something to happen and it isn't happening yet—or wants something to stop and it doesn't—and build the scene around that delay.
When a character's old fear is about to become a present reality, don't relieve the fear; make the situation worse than the character anticipated.
Consciously create moments in which the reader feels tension. Remember that your job is to give readers stress, strain, and pressure—readers love in fiction what they hate in life.
Distinguish tension from suspense in your pacing: use tension in brief bursts that last seconds or minutes, and let suspense carry the long arc of the work.
Create tension by causing friction: have a character resist a demand or order, and keep the resistance going, because the tension lasts only as long as the disobedience.
Cut the immediate relief of your character’s pressing problem: don’t resolve it at once, but stretch the tension out as long as possible.
Rewrite your opening to note a single chilling “fact”—something concrete and precise—that alarms the reader on its own.
Place the first moment of tension as close to the beginning of your work as possible—it puts you in charge of the reader’s emotions.
After your early pages have fastened the reader to a character, create moments of tension for that character as soon as possible.
Describe a character’s dangerous work in minute detail so the reader feels tension mount with every turn of the screw.
Give the scene a deadline and show it closing in—at four o’clock panic, at two minutes to six extreme tension—until the last-moment arrival.
Put your character in an unavoidable meeting with a dangerous figure from their past, and let the reader grow tense instantly.
Pile one tense moment on another, adding to the degree of tension toward a climax instead of ending the confrontation at once.
Before the confrontation pays off, insert a complication—a volunteer who fumbles the rifle, a missing flashlight—that stretches the tension out.
Build moments of high tension even when the outcome is already known: stretch out the moments in which the reader hopes the character will stop, change course, not go through with it.
Relocate a sentence in your scene—transpose it to a later position and re-paragraph around it—to increase tension without changing a word.
Write dialogue that sparks with friction, generating tension in the reader the way it does in life.
When a word is overused in your text, consult a thesaurus that offers near misses and far-off synonyms, and use them to add color as well as diversity.
Diminish a coincidence by having a third character stage the “accidental” meeting at an event that third character arranges.
Check whether your title insulates your book from the public; if it does not arouse a reader’s interest or promise a rich experience, revise it.
Stand in a bookstore and study the titles of books by authors you don’t know; note which titles tempt you to pick the books up and which don’t, then judge your own title by the same standard.
Look past the short-description title for your nonfiction work and find the more imaginative title that would appeal to readers.
Look for your title in the lines of poems and songs that resonate with your book’s theme and audience.
Choose a title early that people respond to, and let that response spur you to complete the work.
Make your title a metaphor: put two things together that don’t ordinarily go together, so the title intrigues and exercises the reader’s imagination.
Title your novel with the leading character’s name plus an energizing factor rather than the bare name.
Consider each word of your title carefully: even words that mean the same thing can make or break the book, so test synonymous rewordings against each other.
Remember that a title’s primary function is not to convey meaning but to sound enticing and exude resonance; test your title against that standard.
Look forward to rewriting: treat your first draft as material to excise and improve, not as finished.
Remove any self-imposed limit on how much rewriting you will do.
Do not revise front-to-back: sort the problems in your manuscript and attend to major matters first.
Print a hard copy of your manuscript to consult while revising — seeing your words on paper gives you a fresh impression — and reprint each section after major changes so you work from clean copy.
Test your main characters: if you cannot think of an important character in situations away from the story, that character needs more work.
If your protagonist is too like yourself, give the character a distinctive trait — positive or negative — that you are sure you do not have.
Add some sparkle to your main character — an interesting eccentricity, a personality characteristic that makes his company enjoyable — because you are asking the reader to spend hours with him.
Imagine you have just won a two-million-dollar lottery and your character hears about it on the news; use his reactions to make him more interesting.
Humanize your characters by giving them the kind of thoughts people have in life — not always "nice" thoughts.
Make your protagonist undergo change in the course of the novel; if yours does not, revise it so that it does.
Keep to a single villain or antagonist; more than one diffuses the impact of the villainy.
Deepen the degree of your antagonist's villainy: is he morally bad rather than just badly behaved, malicious rather than mischievous?
Give your villain something that charms or entices people — charm, charisma, position, or wealth — or he cannot attract victims.
If your villain is hard to make charming or interesting, try seeing him through the eyes of someone who loves him; a humanized villain is a more effective adversary.
Do not model a villain on an enemy from your life: novels are not a place to get even — create characters more interesting than the nasties you know.
Give each minor character one special characteristic, or characterize them through one of the senses you have neglected.
Make sure you have a credible conflict between protagonist and antagonist; a plot needs people overcoming obstacles against high odds and strong adversaries.
Name your most memorable scene without looking at the manuscript — if you cannot remember it, it is not memorable — then name your least memorable scene.
Cut your least memorable scene; if cutting it removes information the reader needs, convey that information in an existing scene instead.
Subject the new least memorable scene to the same scrutiny: would the book be stronger without it? Keep cutting until every remaining scene contributes.
If you cannot find a weak scene, put the manuscript aside for a week, a month, or longer — the longer the better — then look again; the weakest scene will jump out.
From memory, jot down the three most important actions in your novel and test whether each is motivated in a way you would accept if someone else told the story.
Establish the motivation of an action by planting it ahead of the scene in which the action takes place.
Plant an object like a gun much earlier than its use, so the use becomes almost inevitable; derive suspense from its not being used when the reader expects it.
Replace coincidence with motivated action: motivation is not an option but a necessity, and coincidence is the mark of transient works.
Review every significant action for character consistency; fix any action not in keeping with the character, or that sounds farfetched, by planting a motive in a prior scene.

Read the first page as if it were written by a contemporary author you admire, then ask: is there a compelling reason to go on to page two? If not, your opening has not sparked the reader's curiosity.
Read the manuscript from page one to the end as a reader and an editor, not as a writer — critically, like a tough editor.
When in doubt about a change, do not make it; note it for later consideration, and expect most of those notes to be discarded.
Tighten the manuscript: overwriting in first drafts is normal — the skill is recognizing on a later reading what can be eliminated and having the guts to cut it.
When unsure whether a paragraph contributes, block-move it to the end of the manuscript; later, restore only the paragraphs that earn their place.
Eliminate between-the-scenes material — the offstage recounting of actions not seen — or make such material active and interesting in itself.
Cut whatever seems not absolutely necessary, and watch for places where your own attention flags — that is usually a sign something needs to be revised or cut.
Vary the length of your sentences; ideally follow an especially long sentence with a short, even abrupt one, but avoid a mechanical short-long-short-long pattern.
Break an unbroken mellifluous cadence — a lovely rhythm, kept up, will put a reader to sleep.
Be relentless in moving the story forward; where it bogs down and you cannot see an immediate fix, mark the place in the margin, write down what may be wrong, and come back to it later.
Mark any section where you catch the author talking or a mix of points of view, and revise it.
Keep your characters under stress from time to time, and make the stress increase — fiction deals with the most stressful moments of the characters' lives.
Cut every unessential adjective and adverb; cut "very"; make every word count.
If you have said the same thing twice in different words, cut the weaker one; swap a repeated uncommon word for a synonym; and mark every cliché for excision.
Put the speaker identification first ("George said") whenever there is any chance the reader will not know who is speaking; otherwise let it follow or omit it.
Transpose the order of words, phrases, or clauses in a sentence to let its emphasis fall where you want it.
Transpose words when their order could make a reader momentarily misread the sentence, so the first reading is the correct one.
Remove conspicuous passages you love — images and sentences that jump off the page and interfere with the story — and save them in a special box to look into years later.
Root out sentimentality — an excess of response to a stimulus — and underplay to evoke emotion in the reader.
Make sure there is something visual on every page: mark V in the corner of pages that have a visual element and NV on pages that do not, then return to introduce a visual element on every NV page.
If your characters usually speak in complete sentences, fix it so they don't.
Break up any dialogue that runs longer than three sentences with an interjection, thought, or action, and make responses oblique at least from time to time.
Catch every place a character "muttered" or "screamed" instead of "said," and substitute "he said" and "she said" — the dialogue, not the tag, should tell how lines are spoken.
Make a checklist of everything to catch during your general revision; if you cannot do it all in one pass, save some items for a second pass.
Consider whether bringing a strong scene forward would provoke the reader's curiosity more than the scene that presently starts the book.
Make the ending of your book a high point of satisfaction for the reader; if it is not, consider whether another scene or circumstance would make a better ending.

For a final read-through, work with a clean manuscript in which your changes are not visible, and fix anything that momentarily makes you see words on the page and takes you out of experiencing the story.
Replace vague phrases like “a regular guy” — verbal trunks into which a hundred readers pile their own meanings — and say exactly what you mean.
Make sure something visible appears on every page: pencil a V in the corner of each page that has something visual, and on pages without a V, create something visual.
Ask whether your opening is sufficiently visual for the reader to see it; if not, make it visual.
Create suspense by raising a question and withholding the answer for a while; find a place in the piece where you can do this now.
Attend to the individual meaning and resonance of every word and show respect for the reader’s intelligence — that attention is what separates literary writing from commercial.
Bring two words together that have not been together before — achieve precision by creating a new grouping of words rather than using each word only for its exact meaning.
Write down what you see in your most secret snapshot — and if you’re tempted to fudge or invent one, change it to the snapshot you’re actually hiding.
